faq.q: Is German language required for DAAD RISE Germany?
faq.a: No. Most projects operate in English, and German is not required, though a few basic phrases help outside the laboratory.

faq.q: When is the DAAD RISE Germany deadline?
faq.a: The project database typically opens in mid-October and applications close at the end of November, with recommendation letters due shortly after.

faq.q: What if I study outside the eligible countries?
faq.a: Indian undergraduates can apply through DAAD WISE, and students from many other countries may be eligible for DAAD RISE Worldwide, which follows a similar model.

posts.title: IAESTE Internships: Paid Work Abroad for STEM
posts.metaDescription: IAESTE internships give STEM students paid work experience abroad in 80+ countries. Learn how the exchange works, who can apply, and how to get a placement.
posts.excerpt: A guide to IAESTE internships: paid STEM traineeships abroad through a national committee, covering eligibility, funding, the application process and practical tips.
posts.bodyHtml:
IAESTE internships are among the longest-running and most reliable ways for STEM students to earn real work experience abroad. IAESTE, the International Association for the Exchange of Students for Technical Experience, has been arranging paid technical traineeships since 1948, and today its network spans more than 80 member countries. If you are studying engineering, computer science, mathematics or the natural sciences, an IAESTE placement can give you paid work in a company, university or research institute on the other side of the world.

This guide explains what IAESTE actually does, who can apply, how the exchange model works, and how to move through the application process step by step. The single biggest mistake students make with IAESTE is misunderstanding how the system works, so we will make that clear first.

Key takeaways

  • IAESTE arranges paid technical traineeships for STEM students in more than 80 countries.
  • Most placements last 8 to 12 weeks over the summer, though longer internships are available.
  • You apply through your national IAESTE committee, not directly to a central portal.
  • Host employers pay a salary or stipend designed to cover local living costs.
  • The receiving committee helps with housing, insurance and a social programme for interns.

What is IAESTE and how does it work?

IAESTE is a non-profit organisation built on a reciprocal exchange model. A company or university in one member country offers a paid traineeship, and an IAESTE national committee in another country sends a qualified student to fill it. In return, the sending country expects to receive interns for its own employers. This give-and-take keeps the system fair and means that even students from countries with fewer local opportunities can access placements elsewhere.

In practice, you do not apply directly to employers for most positions. Instead, your national committee matches your profile to the offers available to your country and nominates you, which is why contacting your local IAESTE committee early is essential.

Who can apply?

IAESTE internships are aimed at students currently enrolled in a bachelor's, master's or PhD programme, and some committees also accept recent graduates, typically within about a year of finishing. The core focus is STEM: engineering, science, mathematics, information technology and related technical fields. Some positions are open to students from other disciplines, but the vast majority are technical.

You do not need to be a citizen of a member country to apply, but you usually apply through the committee in the country where you study, so check how your institution or country is connected to the network.

Are IAESTE internships really paid?

Yes. IAESTE internships are paid, but the important word is sustainable rather than lucrative. Host employers provide a salary or stipend calculated to cover the local cost of living, so the exact amount varies enormously by country and position. A placement in Switzerland will pay far more in absolute terms than one in Brazil, but both are normally enough for a student to live on during the internship.

Housing is typically arranged or subsidised by the receiving committee, and many committees organise welcome activities, trips and a social programme so interns from different countries meet each other. That combination, a living wage, accommodation support and a built-in community, is what makes an IAESTE summer genuinely affordable.

How to apply step by step

The process is slightly different in every country, but it follows the same broad pattern.

Step 1: Find and register

Search open internship offers on the IAESTE website and register on the exchange platform. Once registered, your national committee can see your profile and match you to offers.

Step 2: Contact your national committee

Your committee guides you through the application, tells you which offers are available to your country, and helps you prepare the required documents, typically a cover letter, CV, transcripts and sometimes language certificates.

Step 3: Get nominated and accepted

If the committee selects you for an offer, your documents are forwarded to the employer, who makes the final decision. Once accepted, you receive details about your start date, insurance and accommodation, and the committee helps with visa paperwork where needed.

What documents do you need?

Prepare a strong cover letter and an up-to-date CV that highlights relevant coursework, projects and technical skills. Many committees also ask for academic transcripts and evidence of English proficiency, since English is the working language for most positions even when the host country speaks another language. If you are unsure how to structure a persuasive motivation letter, our guide to writing a winning statement of purpose covers techniques that apply here too.

Visas and insurance

Because you travel as a trainee rather than a student, visa rules differ from country to country. Some placements are short enough to fall under a visitor visa, while longer internships require a specific work or training visa. The receiving IAESTE committee coordinates most of this, but start early and keep copies of every document. For a general overview of what the process involves, see our student visa guide.

Making the most of your placement

An IAESTE internship is as much about the experience as the salary. Interns come away with real technical experience, an international network and a CV that stands out to graduate programmes and employers. Take part in the social programme, keep a record of the projects you work on, and ask your supervisor for feedback and a reference at the end.

How to apply: next steps

Start by finding the IAESTE office for your country on iaeste.org and asking how the local cycle works, because committees often have their own application windows and deadlines. Prepare your documents, register on the platform, and check the open internships regularly so you can signal interest in the offers that fit you best.

Then treat your IAESTE application with the same seriousness as a job interview, because that is effectively what it is. For more funded international work experience ideas, browse our internships hub and our playbook for funded summer research internships abroad.

faq.q: What is IAESTE?
faq.a: IAESTE, the International Association for the Exchange of Students for Technical Experience, arranges paid technical traineeships for STEM students in more than 80 countries through national committees.

faq.q: Are IAESTE internships paid?
faq.a: Yes. Host employers provide a salary or stipend calculated to cover local living costs, and the amount varies by country and position.

faq.q: Who can apply for IAESTE internships?
faq.a: Current undergraduate, master's or PhD students in STEM fields, and some committees also accept recent graduates, usually within about a year of finishing.

faq.q: How do I apply for an IAESTE internship?
faq.a: You register on the IAESTE platform and apply through your national committee, which matches your profile to offers available to your country and handles nominations.

faq.q: How long do IAESTE internships last?
faq.a: Most placements last 8 to 12 weeks over the summer, though longer internships are available in some countries.

posts.title: UN Internships 2026: How to Get a Paid Internship
posts.metaDescription: Which UN internships pay in 2026, who is eligible, stipend ranges by agency, and how to build an application that gets shortlisted.
posts.excerpt: A 2026 guide to paid UN internships at UNICEF, UNDP, UNHCR and beyond, covering stipends, eligibility, where to apply and how to win.
posts.bodyHtml:
UN internships are a common goal for students interested in international development, human rights and global policy, and in 2026 more of them are paid than many people assume. The United Nations runs internships across dozens of agencies and field offices, and several of the best-known bodies, UNICEF, UNDP, UNHCR and WHO, advertise paid roles year-round for students and recent graduates from anywhere in the world. The catch is that the system is decentralised: each agency posts its own vacancies, sets its own eligibility rules and decides its own pay.

This guide cuts through the confusion and explains which UN internships pay in 2026, roughly how much, who is eligible, where to apply, and how to build an application that actually gets read.

Key takeaways

  • UN internships are open to students and recent graduates of all nationalities, with no citizenship requirement.
  • UNICEF pays a monthly stipend of around $1,000 (varies by duty station) plus a one-time travel contribution.
  • UNDP and UNHCR pay stipends to interns who are not otherwise sponsored; WHO and FAO also pay, at varying rates.
  • Parts of the UN Secretariat still advertise unpaid roles, so always read the vacancy before applying.
  • Internships typically last two to six months (UNICEF: six to 26 weeks) and can be in person, hybrid or remote.

Which UN internships pay in 2026?

This is the question everyone asks first, and the honest answer is that it depends on the agency. The big, frequently hiring agencies mostly pay, with stipends set by duty station:

  • UNICEF: around $1,000 per month, plus a one-time lump sum toward travel and visa costs when funding is available. Roles are posted on UNICEF's careers site year-round.
  • UNDP: a monthly stipend set by duty station and work arrangement (including a remote tier), paid to interns who are not already funded by a university or other sponsor. Vacancies appear on jobs.undp.org on a rolling basis.
  • UNHCR: a mandatory stipend for interns without external funding, plus reimbursement of return travel for eligible interns travelling from abroad.
  • WHO and FAO: paid internship schemes with stipends roughly in the $700–1,800 per month range depending on location.
  • Parts of the UN Secretariat: some offices still advertise unpaid internships, so the pay status should be checked on every individual vacancy.

Eligibility

Most UN agencies accept interns who are enrolled in an undergraduate or graduate degree program, or who graduated within the past two years (some agencies accept up to one year). You usually need to be at least eighteen and fluent in at least one working language, most often English. Interns are not UN staff; the arrangement is an experiential learning opportunity, which is exactly why funding policies vary so much across the system.

Where and how to apply

There is no single UN application form. UNICEF posts on unicef.org/careers, UNDP on jobs.undp.org, UNHCR on unhcr.org/careers, WHO on its careers portal, and many bodies also advertise on the central careers.un.org site. Each vacancy has its own deadline, so the practical approach is to check the agency portals regularly and apply to roles that genuinely match your background. Vacancies close when filled, so applying within days of a posting is a real advantage.

Building a strong UN application

UN recruiters read a lot of generic applications, and specificity wins. Tailor your CV and cover letter to the exact duty station, team and mandate of the vacancy, and name the agency's current programmes where relevant. Quantify your experience: instead of "assisted with events", write "coordinated logistics for a fifty-participant workshop". Our guides on writing a winning statement of purpose and building a competitive scholarship profile cover the same skills, and they transfer directly to UN applications.

Practical considerations

Even with a stipend, intern pay rarely covers the full cost of living in cities like Geneva or New York, so plan your budget before you accept an offer. Ask whether the role is in person, hybrid or remote, and clarify visa support early, because agencies vary in how much they can help with paperwork. And be realistic: a UN internship is a strong credential and a networking opportunity, but it does not guarantee a UN job afterwards, so treat it as one step in a longer plan rather than a destination.

How to apply: next steps

Build a clean, tailored CV and a cover letter template now, then start scanning the UNICEF, UNDP, UNHCR and WHO portals. Identify three or four roles that fit your profile, write each application individually, and submit within the first week of each vacancy being posted. If you are not selected, reapply for the next cycle, as many successful UN interns applied several times. For more funded international opportunities, browse our internships hub.

faq.q: Are UN internships paid in 2026?
faq.a: Mostly yes at the big agencies. UNICEF pays around $1,000 per month plus a travel contribution, UNDP and UNHCR pay interns who are not otherwise sponsored, and WHO and FAO have paid schemes. Parts of the UN Secretariat still advertise unpaid roles, so check each vacancy.

faq.q: Who is eligible for a UN internship?
faq.a: Students enrolled in an undergraduate or graduate degree program, or recent graduates (typically within two years), of any nationality. You usually need to be at least 18 and fluent in at least one UN working language, most often English.

faq.q: How long do UN internships last?
faq.a: Most run two to six months. UNICEF internships run six to 26 weeks, and some agencies allow longer periods for academic credit or national service arrangements.

faq.q: Where do I apply for UN internships?
faq.a: You apply separately to each agency: UNICEF on unicef.org/careers, UNDP on jobs.undp.org, UNHCR on unhcr.org/careers, WHO on its careers portal, and many bodies also advertise on careers.un.org.

faq.q: Does a UN internship lead to a UN job?
faq.a: Not automatically. It is a strong credential and networking opportunity, but entry-level UN positions are extremely competitive. Treat it as one step in a longer career plan rather than a guaranteed doorway.

posts.title: NASA Internships & L'SPACE Academy Guide
posts.metaDescription: NASA internships and L'SPACE Academy explained: who is eligible, what it really is, and the best funded alternatives for international space students.
posts.excerpt: What NASA internships and the L'SPACE Academy actually require, why international students are usually excluded, and the funded alternatives that work.
posts.bodyHtml:
NASA internships are the dream of many STEM students, and NASA's flagship student internship programme offers some of the most sought-after placements in the world. But there is an uncomfortable fact that most articles skip: NASA internships are generally limited to US citizens, and the popular L'SPACE Academy also requires US citizenship or permanent residency. If you are an international student, knowing the real rules before you apply will save you time and point you toward the routes that are actually open to you.

This guide explains how NASA internships work, what L'SPACE Academy is, and what international students should do instead if they want to break into the space industry.

Key takeaways

  • NASA's central internship programme is open to US citizens, with international access only through rare formal arrangements.
  • L'SPACE Academy is a free, online training programme for US citizens and permanent residents at US colleges and universities.
  • L'SPACE is not an internship; it is project-based training that strengthens applications for real internships.
  • International students can build space careers through national agencies, IAESTE and funded research programmes.
  • Always check citizenship requirements on every posting before investing time in an application.

How NASA internships actually work

NASA's student internship programme, run through the STEM Gateway portal at stemgateway.nasa.gov, places students at NASA centers across the United States, from Goddard to JPL. Interns work with NASA mentors on real projects, are paid, and can return for multiple terms. Applications open three times a year for fall, spring and summer sessions, and summer is by far the most competitive.

The eligibility rule is the part that matters most for international students. NASA internships require US citizenship for almost all positions. A small number of arrangements exist for international students at certain centers or through formal partnerships, but they are rare and usually channelled through universities or national agencies rather than open applications.

What is L'SPACE Academy?

L'SPACE, the NASA Lucy Student Pipeline Accelerator and Competency Enabler, is a free, fully online programme run by Arizona State University as the official student collaboration program for NASA's Lucy mission. It was created to train the next generation of the space workforce by teaching students how NASA actually plans, designs and reviews missions.

Eligibility is strict: you must be a US citizen or permanent resident, enrolled in a US college or university as an undergraduate or graduate student. International students studying in the US on a student visa are not eligible.

The two academies

L'SPACE has two academies. The Mission Concept Academy (MCA) takes undergraduates through a full mission design cycle, from requirements to a preliminary design review. The NASA Proposal Writing and Evaluation Experience (NPWEE) teaches how real NASA proposals are written and evaluated. Students typically complete one academy per semester, and each runs for about twelve to fifteen weeks with a significant time commitment.

Why L'SPACE matters even though it is unpaid

L'SPACE is not an internship and pays no stipend, but alumni consistently report that it changed their career trajectory. You learn mission procedures from people who have worked on real missions, you collaborate with students from across the US, and you finish with portfolio-ready deliverables such as mission concept documents and proposal reviews. Many alumni go on to internships at NASA, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman and other space employers.

For students who are eligible, L'SPACE is one of the highest-value free investments you can make in a space career. For international students, the programme itself is closed, but the skills it teaches are not, and you can learn the same fundamentals through free NASA resources, open coursework and project work.

What international students should do instead

If you cannot access NASA directly, you still have several genuine routes into space science and engineering.

Use your own national space ecosystem

Most space-faring countries have an agency or institute that runs student internships: ESA in Europe, JAXA in Japan, the Canadian Space Agency, and national agencies across Africa, Asia and Latin America. Many of these hire international students or students from partner countries, and some fund the placement.

Use funded international programmes

Programmes like IAESTE and DAAD RISE Germany place STEM undergraduates in research groups and companies abroad, and space-related placements appear in their offer lists. These are genuinely open to international students and are often fully or partly funded.

Build a space profile online

NASA publishes enormous amounts of free material, from open data and citizen science projects to course-like resources and virtual challenges. Working on an open-source space project, entering a space hackathon, or analysing NASA open data gives you similar portfolio material to L'SPACE alumni, without the citizenship requirement.

How to apply: next steps

If you are a US citizen or permanent resident, create a profile on stemgateway.nasa.gov for NASA internships and apply through lspace.asu.edu for L'SPACE. If you are an international student, skip the NASA portal and instead register with your national space agency, check IAESTE and DAAD RISE offers, and start a portfolio project that demonstrates your skills.

Whichever route you take, remember that space careers reward demonstrated ability more than titles. For a wider view of what you are eligible for, read our guide to finding opportunities you can actually apply to, and browse our internships hub.

faq.q: Are NASA internships open to international students?
faq.a: Almost always no. NASA's central internship programme requires US citizenship, and international access exists only through rare formal arrangements.

faq.q: What is the L'SPACE Academy?
faq.a: L'SPACE is a free, online training programme run by Arizona State University for the NASA Lucy mission, with two academies, MCA and NPWEE. It is not an internship.

faq.q: Who can apply to L'SPACE Academy?
faq.a: US citizens and permanent residents enrolled at US colleges or universities as undergraduate or graduate students; international students on student visas are not eligible.

faq.q: Is L'SPACE paid?
faq.a: No. L'SPACE is unpaid training, but alumni use the project work to strengthen applications for NASA and space-industry internships.

faq.q: What should international students apply to instead?
faq.a: Options include their national space agency, IAESTE, DAAD RISE Germany and open-source space projects, all of which are open to international students.

posts.title: Erasmus+ Traineeships: Paid Internships in Europe
posts.metaDescription: Erasmus+ traineeships fund internships in Europe for students. Learn who is eligible, what the grant covers, and how to apply through your university.
posts.excerpt: A practical guide to Erasmus+ traineeships: who can take part, what the grant covers, how to find a host organisation, and how to apply through your university.
posts.bodyHtml:
Erasmus+ traineeships are one of the most accessible funded internship routes in Europe, yet they are widely misunderstood. Erasmus+ is the European Union's flagship programme for education, training and mobility, and its traineeship strand funds higher education students to complete an internship in another participating country. Because the money flows through universities rather than through employers, an Erasmus+ traineeship is usually easier to arrange and more affordable than a conventional internship abroad.

This guide explains who can take part, what the grant covers, how to find a host organisation, and how to apply through your own university.

Key takeaways

  • Erasmus+ traineeships fund internships in another programme country for students at participating universities.
  • Eligibility is tied to your university, not your nationality, so many international students can take part.
  • You apply through your home university's international office, which manages the funding allocation.
  • The grant is a monthly contribution based on the host country's living costs, sometimes topped up for travel.
  • Host organisations can be companies, research institutes, NGOs or universities.

What is an Erasmus+ traineeship?

An Erasmus+ traineeship is a period of practical work abroad, typically two to twelve months, completed by a higher education student as part of their degree. The student finds, or is helped to find, a host organisation in another participating country, and their home university supports the placement with an Erasmus+ grant funded through the European Commission.

The arrangement is flexible by design. Traineeships can happen during term time where the curriculum allows, but for most students they happen in the summer. You can work in a company, a research group, a hospital, an NGO or a public institution, as long as the placement is related to your field of study and counts toward your learning goals.

Who can take part?

Eligibility depends on where you study, not where you come from. You must be enrolled in a higher education institution that holds an Erasmus+ charter, which covers essentially all universities in the EU member states and the other programme countries: Iceland, Liechtenstein, North Macedonia, Norway, Serbia and Türkiye.

Can international students take part?

Yes, in most cases. International students enrolled at a participating European university can usually join Erasmus+ traineeships on the same terms as local students, provided they hold the right visa or residence status for the host country. The university's international office can confirm whether your specific situation qualifies, so always ask before planning.

Note that Erasmus+ traineeships are different from Erasmus Mundus joint master's programmes, which are full degree scholarships. Traineeships are short funding windows within your existing degree.

What does the grant cover?

The Erasmus+ grant is a monthly contribution toward the cost of living abroad, and the amount depends on the host country, with higher rates for more expensive destinations. Students with fewer opportunities, such as those from disadvantaged backgrounds or with disabilities, can sometimes receive a top-up, and a small travel contribution may also be available.

The grant is not a salary and is not designed to replace wages; it typically covers a significant share of rent and living costs. Some host organisations also pay the intern a wage on top, which can make the placement genuinely comfortable. Always confirm the exact grant amount for your destination and the rules of your university's allocation.

How to find a host organisation

You have two main paths. Many universities maintain lists of partner organisations that already accept Erasmus+ trainees, which simplifies paperwork. Alternatively, you can approach an employer or research group yourself and ask whether they would host an Erasmus+ trainee; because the grant covers your living costs, many organisations are willing to take on an intern even without an internal budget.

A cold email that explains the Erasmus+ funding model and your relevant skills works well here. Frame it as a proposal that costs the host little, and attach a focused CV.

How to apply step by step

The process is managed by your university, so start with its international office.

Step 1: Confirm eligibility and quotas

Ask your international office whether you are eligible, how many traineeship grants are available this year, and what deadlines apply. Grants are often allocated in rounds, and competition exists for the most popular destinations.

Step 2: Find your placement

Secure a host organisation and agree the dates, tasks and expected learning outcomes. A written acceptance from the host is usually required.

Step 3: Complete the paperwork

You sign a learning agreement that sets out the internship plan, and your university confirms the grant amount and insurance arrangements. The European Commission also provides an online language course to help you prepare for working in the host country's language.

Practical tips

Start planning at least a semester ahead, because grants are limited and paperwork takes time. Choose a placement that genuinely fits your studies, since the learning agreement ties the internship to your degree, and keep your receipts, because the grant may be paid in instalments linked to your progress reports.

If an Erasmus+ traineeship alone is not enough to fund your year abroad, you can combine it with other support. Our guide to funding your studies abroad without a full scholarship explains how to layer funding sources safely and legally.

How to apply: next steps

Book an appointment with your university's international office this month and ask three questions: am I eligible, what is the grant for my target country, and what is the application deadline? In parallel, research host organisations and prepare a short proposal email. Once your placement is secured and the paperwork is signed, you are set for a funded internship in Europe.

For a wider list of options, browse our internships hub and our playbook for funded summer research internships abroad.

posts.title: OECD Internships & Junior Professional Programme
posts.metaDescription: OECD internships and the Junior Professional Programme explained: eligibility for all nationalities, funding, the application process, and how to stand out.
posts.excerpt: A guide to paid opportunities at the OECD: the internship programme and the Junior Professional Programme, covering eligibility, funding and applications.
posts.bodyHtml:
The OECD offers two distinct ways to build an international career in economic and social policy: a well-known internship programme and a more advanced entry route called the Junior Professional Programme (JPP). Both are open to candidates of all nationalities, which makes them genuinely different from many government organisations, and both are funded. The OECD, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, is based in Paris and works on policy across nearly forty member countries plus many partner economies, so interns and junior professionals join a genuinely global policy environment.

This guide explains how OECD internships work, what the Junior Professional Programme is, who is eligible for each, and how to make your application competitive.

Key takeaways

  • OECD internships are open to candidates of all nationalities who are enrolled in a degree or have recently graduated.
  • Interns receive a monthly allowance designed to cover living costs in Paris.
  • The Junior Professional Programme is a paid two-year fixed-term role for recent graduates, open to candidates of all OECD member and partner countries.
  • Both routes are based mainly in Paris, though some assignments are hybrid or in field offices.
  • Applications go through oecd.org/careers, and competitive candidates show strong analytical and language skills.

How OECD internships work

The OECD internship programme places students in its policy directorates, where they contribute to research, analysis, event support and communications. Interns work with experienced analysts on projects that feed into real OECD output, such as country reviews, working papers and statistical reports. Assignments typically run from one to six months and can sometimes be renewed, with many interns joining for three months over the summer.

Eligibility is broad. You need to be enrolled in a full-time degree programme or to have graduated within the past two years, and you should have a good command of one of the OECD's working languages, most often English, with French a strong advantage. There is no age limit and no citizenship requirement.

Is the OECD internship paid?

Yes. OECD interns receive a monthly allowance intended to cover the cost of living in Paris, which is widely reported to be around one thousand euros per month, though you should confirm the current figure on the official programme page. Interns are also expected to arrange their own accommodation and travel, so the allowance is a contribution rather than a full salary. You are not an employee of the OECD, and the internship does not automatically lead to a staff contract, though it is an excellent entry signal.

What is the Junior Professional Programme?

The Junior Professional Programme is the OECD's structured route for recent graduates who want to work at the organisation. It is a paid, two-year fixed-term appointment at a junior analyst level, and JPP participants carry real responsibility from the start, contributing to directorate work, country reviews and policy research. The salary is a proper OECD salary with benefits, not an intern allowance.

The programme is open to candidates from all OECD member countries and partner economies, and to both university graduates and those with a few years of early-career experience. Selection is competitive and usually involves an online assessment and interviews, and participants are expected to relocate to Paris unless the assignment is elsewhere.

How the application process works

Both routes are managed through the OECD careers website at oecd.org/careers, and the process for each is different.

Applying for an internship

Internship vacancies are posted on the OECD careers site, often with rolling deadlines. Create a profile, upload a tailored CV and cover letter, and apply to specific openings rather than submitting a general application. Because demand for OECD internships is high, applications that connect the applicant's coursework to a specific directorate's priorities stand out.

Applying for the JPP

The Junior Professional Programme has its own recruitment cycle, with applications opening for a defined period each year. The process typically includes an online application with motivation questions, a technical assessment, and structured interviews. Prepare by studying the OECD's current priorities, from climate and digitalisation to education and employment, and be ready to discuss how your skills map to real OECD projects.

Making your application competitive

The OECD works in policy analysis, so your application needs to demonstrate analytical writing. Highlight coursework, theses or prior work where you handled data, wrote policy briefs or produced research reports, and name the relevant OECD work streams you would like to contribute to. Language skills matter, so list every language you can work in, not just the ones you are fluent in.

Your cover letter should read like a short statement of purpose, explaining why the OECD, why this team and why you. Our guide to writing a winning statement of purpose walks through the same structure, and our advice on building a competitive profile applies directly to international applications like this one.

Practical considerations

Paris is an expensive city, so budget carefully before accepting an internship, and start your visa research early if you need one. The OECD can provide documentation to support visa applications, but the responsibility for obtaining a visa sits with you. For a general walkthrough, see our student visa guide.

Both the internship and the JPP reward persistence. The OECD receives thousands of applications for a limited number of places, so it is normal not to be selected on the first attempt, and many successful candidates applied across several cycles.

How to apply: next steps

Create your profile on oecd.org/careers this week and set up a calendar reminder to check new internship postings. Identify two or three directorates that fit your interests, tailor your CV and cover letter to each, and apply early in the cycle. If you meet the JPP eligibility window, prepare your application materials well before the deadline and practise for the assessment.

While you wait, keep building the skills the OECD values. For more funded policy and research opportunities, browse our internships hub and our guide to funded summer research internships abroad.

faq.a: Not automatically, but they build strong networks and policy skills, and JPP roles are a recognised entry route into the organisation.

posts.title: Google Internships: How to Apply & Get Hired
posts.metaDescription: How to apply for Google internships: eligible roles, rolling deadlines, technical and non-technical interview prep, and how to build a standout profile.
posts.excerpt: A practical guide to Google internships covering eligible roles, application timing, the interview process, and how to build a profile that gets read.
posts.bodyHtml:
Google internships are famously competitive, but they are also more systematic than most students expect. Google hires thousands of interns each year across software engineering, product management, UX design, marketing, data science and many other fields, and the selection process follows a clear, repeatable path. Understanding that path, and preparing for it months in advance, is what separates students who reach the interviews from those who never hear back.

This guide covers what Google internships look like, who is eligible, how the application and interview process works, and how to build a candidate profile that survives the screening stage.

Key takeaways

  • Google internships span software engineering, STEP, product management, UX, data science and business roles.
  • Internships are paid, typically last twelve to fourteen weeks over the summer, and include housing support or a stipend.
  • You apply online at careers.google.com, and most teams review applications on a rolling basis in the fall.
  • Software interviews are technical and focus on algorithms, data structures and coding on a shared editor.
  • Non-technical roles test product sense, communication and structured problem solving in case-style interviews.

The range of Google internships

Most people know Google for software engineering, but the internship programme covers nearly every part of the company. On the technical side, there are software engineering internships for generalists, hardware roles, and the STEP (Student Training in Engineering Program) internship aimed at first- and second-year students. On the non-technical side, Google hires interns in product management, UX design, program management, data science, marketing and business strategy.

Because hiring is decentralised, each team posts its own internships on the careers site, with its own requirements and timeline. Some roles are remote or hybrid, but most technical internships are on-site at a Google office, and you typically work on a real project with a host team and a dedicated intern mentor.

Who is eligible?

Requirements vary by role, but the common baseline is current enrolment in a relevant bachelor's, master's or PhD programme, with recent graduates sometimes eligible for a limited window. There is no single citizenship rule for Google internships, which is a big difference from government and space programmes; instead, the practical constraint is work authorisation for the office location, and Google's internship team handles the specifics with each candidate.

That means an international student can absolutely intern at Google, including at offices in the United States and Europe, as long as the visa logistics work out. Start visa conversations early, because they can take months.

Are Google internships paid?

Yes, and generously by internship standards. Google interns receive a competitive monthly salary, and for on-site internships the company typically provides furnished housing or a housing stipend, a travel allowance, and other perks such as meals and access to intern events. The compensation is designed to make a summer at Google realistic even if you relocate from abroad, which is precisely why these internships are among the most popular funded opportunities in tech.

How to apply

Applications go through careers.google.com, where you search internships by location and discipline. Because teams hire on a rolling basis, timing is critical: many technical roles open in the early fall for the following summer and start interviewing immediately, so applying in September or October is genuinely different from applying in January. Set up job alerts on the careers site so you see postings the day they go live.

How the interview process works

The process differs between technical and non-technical roles, but it usually follows a similar arc.

Technical interviews

Software engineering and data science candidates complete a coding screen, often through a shared online editor, followed by one or more onsite-style interviews. The focus is on algorithms, data structures and clean problem solving: you are evaluated on how you think, communicate and handle edge cases, not just on whether your code compiles. Practise on a whiteboard or shared editor, explain your reasoning out loud, and do at least a few timed mock interviews before the real thing.

Non-technical interviews

Product management, UX and business interns face case-style interviews that test product sense, prioritisation and analytical thinking. Expect questions like "how would you improve a product for a specific audience" or "how would you measure the success of a new feature". Prepare a framework, such as goals, users, solutions and metrics, and practise applying it to real Google products and everyday apps.

Building a profile that gets read

Resumes at Google are screened by humans who look for evidence of initiative and impact. Projects beat coursework: a well-documented personal project, an open-source contribution, or a competitive programming record signals more than a high GPA alone. For design and product roles, a portfolio that shows your thinking is essential, and for research-aligned roles, publications and lab experience count heavily.

If your background is thin in one area, build it deliberately. Contributing to an open-source project, completing a rigorous online course, or securing a funded research internship first can give you the projects and references that make your Google application credible.

Common mistakes to avoid

Applying to every role at once dilutes your application; instead, pick two or three internships that genuinely fit your skills and tailor each. Do not wait until the deadline, because rolling hiring means early applications are read first. And do not let a rejection stop you: Google teams rehire constantly, and a strong candidate who applies again the next cycle is completely normal. Our guide to common application mistakes to avoid covers the same patterns in a different context.

How to apply: next steps

Create your careers.google.com profile today and set alerts for the roles that fit you. Then work backwards from the summer: if interviews happen in the fall, your coding practice and portfolio building should be well underway now. Target two or three roles, tailor your resume for each, and schedule at least one mock interview before you apply.

Finally, remember that a Google internship is a launchpad, not a final destination. Whatever the outcome, the interview preparation and project experience will strengthen every other application you make. For more tech and research opportunities abroad, browse our internships hub.

posts.title: How to Get a Funded Research Internship Abroad
posts.metaDescription: How to find and win a funded summer research internship abroad: the main programmes, eligibility filtering, application strategy, and a step-by-step timeline.
posts.excerpt: A strategy guide to funded summer research internships abroad: where the programmes are, how to filter for eligibility, and how to build a winning application.
posts.bodyHtml:
A funded summer research internship abroad is one of the most valuable things an undergraduate can do: paid research experience in another country, a strong reference from an international lab, and a CV that stands apart in graduate school applications. The good news is that more funded programmes exist than most students realise. The challenge is that they are scattered, competitive and deadline-driven, so a systematic approach wins far more often than luck.

This guide walks through the landscape of funded research internships, who is eligible, how to find programmes that fit you, and how to build an application that gets you into a lab abroad.

Key takeaways

  • Funded research internships abroad come from universities, national agencies, bilateral exchanges and international organisations.
  • Programmes typically cover the stipend, housing and often flights, depending on the scheme.
  • Strong programmes include DAAD RISE, IAESTE, the DAAD RISE partner schemes and university-specific summer research fellowships.
  • Apply early: many programmes have deadlines in autumn or early winter for the following summer.
  • A targeted shortlist of five to ten programmes beats mass-applying to fifty.

What a funded research internship looks like

A funded research internship places you in a university lab, research institute or company for a defined period, usually eight to twelve weeks over the summer. You work under a supervisor on a real project, often alongside graduate students, and you produce something concrete by the end: a report, a poster or a piece of analysis. Funding covers a monthly stipend for living costs, and the strongest programmes also arrange or subsidise housing and contribute to international travel.

Compensation varies. Some programmes pay an actual salary, others offer a stipend tied to local living costs, and a few cover only housing plus a small allowance. The label "funded" therefore covers a range, and the right question is not "does it pay?" but "will it cover my costs for the summer?".

The main families of programmes

Funded research internships abroad fall into a few broad families, and knowing them helps you search in the right places.

National agency programmes

Many countries fund international undergraduate research to attract talent and build partnerships. Germany's DAAD RISE Germany is the flagship example, placing students from the United States, Canada, the UK and Ireland in German research groups with full funding. Similar schemes run through national research councils, cultural agencies and government scholarships, and they are often better funded than university programmes.

International exchange organisations

Organisations like IAESTE sit between research and professional training, placing STEM students in paid technical and research placements across more than eighty countries. Because the funding model is reciprocal and employer-based, the money is real and the application runs through your national committee.

University summer research fellowships

Hundreds of universities run funded summer research programmes for students from partner institutions or from abroad. These range from large flagship schemes in the United States, Canada, Australia and Europe to smaller faculty-driven projects, and many are open to international applicants. Search for terms like "summer research fellowship international students" plus a country or university name.

Intergovernmental organisations

Organisations such as the UN agencies, the OECD and the European Commission run funded internship and research placements that suit policy and quantitative fields. These are covered in detail in our guides to UN internships, OECD internships and the Junior Professional Programme, and Erasmus+ traineeships in Europe.

How to find programmes you actually qualify for

The biggest waste of effort is applying to programmes you can never receive, so start by filtering on three things: your citizenship or residence, your year of study, and your field. Read the eligibility section on every official page before anything else, because many programmes are tied to specific countries or degrees. Our guide to finding opportunities you are actually eligible for shows the same filtering method applied to funding.

Then make a spreadsheet. For each programme, record the deadline, the funding, the length, the eligibility rules and the official website. Aim for five to ten strong matches rather than fifty weak ones, and check back in the autumn, because that is when most applications open for the following summer.

Building a competitive research application

Research internship applications are won on evidence of research potential, and the standard package is a CV, a cover letter or statement of interest, transcripts, and usually one or two references. Because most applicants are undergraduates, committees are not expecting published papers; they are looking for signs that you can handle open-ended work, read carefully, and contribute to a lab from week one.

Emphasise project work: lab courses, final-year projects, hackathons, data analysis, even a well-run independent study. Name specific skills honestly, and when a programme asks for a research statement, connect your interests to the work happening in the labs you are applying to. Our guide to writing a winning statement of purpose and our advice on getting strong letters of recommendation apply directly here.

Using research internships strategically

A funded research internship is rarely just a summer job; it is a stepping stone. Interns leave with an international reference, a concrete research sample, and often a paper, poster or dataset they can build on. For students aiming at graduate school, a strong internship abroad is one of the most persuasive signals you can send, and it can lead directly to a master's or PhD offer in the same lab.

Treat the experience that way: ask your supervisor for feedback at the end, keep a record of what you produced, and stay in touch. Many successful applicants to graduate programmes were first interns.

How to apply: next steps

Start this month, not in spring. Build your spreadsheet of programmes with deadlines and eligibility, prepare your CV, transcripts and references, and confirm who can write your recommendation letters early. Then apply to your shortlist the week each application opens, because several programmes review on a rolling basis.

Once you have offers, compare the funding carefully and confirm the visa and insurance steps with the programme office. For the wider picture of what you can fund your studies with afterwards, browse our internships hub and our guide to funding your studies abroad without a full scholarship.

posts.excerpt: A complete guide to study abroad programs for US students: the four main routes, how federal financial aid works overseas, the scholarships worth applying for, and a realistic application timeline.

faq.q: Do I have to go through my home university to study abroad?
faq.a: Not always, but it is almost always the best idea. University-approved programs protect your federal financial aid, make credit transfer straightforward, and are the only route through which your Pell Grant and federal loans can apply.

faq.q: Can I use my Pell Grant when studying abroad?
faq.a: Yes, if you stay enrolled at least half-time in a program your home university approves for credit. As a Pell recipient you are also then eligible for the Benjamin A. Gilman Scholarship, worth up to $5,000 or more.

faq.q: How much does a semester abroad cost?
faq.a: All-in costs typically range from about $8,000 to $20,000. Exchanges where you pay home tuition sit at the low end, while full-service provider programs in expensive cities sit at the top.

faq.q: When should I start applying for study abroad?
faq.a: Start 8 to 12 months ahead. For a fall semester, attend info sessions in the previous September and October, apply to programs between January and March, and file scholarship applications even earlier.

faq.q: What is the difference between an exchange and a provider program?
faq.a: An exchange sends you to a partner university while you keep paying your home tuition. A provider program like CIEE or SIT charges its own program fee but includes housing, excursions, and full-time on-site support.

posts.bodyHtml:
More than a quarter of a million US undergraduates now study abroad every year, according to IIE's Open Doors data, and nearly every American university runs a study abroad office of its own. That breadth is both the good news and the challenge: "study abroad" covers several very different kinds of programs, each with its own cost, credit model, and application process.

This complete guide maps the main study abroad programs for US students, explains how federal financial aid and scholarships apply overseas, and gives you a realistic timeline so you can plan without panic.

Key takeaways

  • Four main routes exist: university exchange, third-party providers, faculty-led courses, and direct enrollment.
  • Exchange programs usually let you pay your home tuition, making them the most affordable path.
  • Federal Pell Grants and Stafford loans can travel abroad if you use an approved, credit-bearing program.
  • The Benjamin A. Gilman Scholarship adds up to $5,000 for Pell-eligible students, more for critical languages or STEM.
  • Providers like CIEE, SIT, API Abroad and IES Abroad charge more but handle almost everything for you.
  • Start working with your study abroad office 8 to 12 months before you want to leave.

The four main types of study abroad programs

Every route below starts at your university's study abroad office, which approves programs, manages credit transfer, and connects you with funding. Which option fits depends on your budget, your language level, and how much structure you want.

University exchange programs

In an exchange, your home school sends you to a partner university abroad and you keep paying your normal home tuition, usually with financial aid applying as if you were still on campus. National networks such as ISEP (isep.org) extend this model through a fee-based membership, giving you hundreds of partner institutions around the world. This is typically the cheapest route, and it protects scholarships that are tied to your home institution.

Third-party provider programs

Providers such as CIEE (ciee.org), SIT Study Abroad (sit.edu), API Abroad (apiabroad.com) and IES Abroad (iesabroad.org) build complete packages: courses, housing, excursions, and full-time on-site staff. You pay their program fee rather than home or host tuition. They cost more than an exchange, but they open up destinations your university may not have partnerships with, and many offer their own grants and early-booking discounts.

Faculty-led and short-term programs

Many departments run 2-to-8-week trips, usually in summer or a January term, taught by your own professors. Credit transfers automatically, logistics are handled by your university, and the price is a fraction of a semester. For many students a short faculty-led trip is the perfect first taste of studying abroad.

Direct enrollment

With direct enrollment you apply to a foreign university as a visiting student, pay its fees, and bring the credit home. In low-tuition countries like Germany this can be dramatically cheaper, as our guide to studying in Germany for free explains. The trade-off is that you arrange visas, housing, and registration yourself.

How US federal financial aid works abroad

Your Pell Grant and Stafford loans generally follow you abroad as long as you stay enrolled at least half-time in a program your home university approves for credit. That approval is the key: study abroad through a program your school does not recognize, and your aid stops. Confirm everything with your financial aid office before you sign anything.

If you receive the Pell Grant, the Benjamin A. Gilman International Scholarship (gilmanscholarship.org) is your first stop, with awards up to $5,000 and up to $8,000 for students studying a critical language or a STEM subject. Gilman is a federal program with a spring and a fall application cycle every year.

Scholarships beyond federal aid

Dedicated funding for US students exists outside Washington too. The Fund for Education Abroad (fundforeducationabroad.org) awards up to $5,000 with a strong focus on students from underrepresented backgrounds. Boren Awards (borenawards.org) fund longer stays for students studying critical languages, in exchange for a year of federal service. Provider programs and most universities also run their own grant rounds, and our scholarships hub lists the main cycles and deadlines.

How to choose the right program

Judge every program on four tests: does the credit count toward your degree, where will you live, how much on-site support is there, and what is the real out-of-pocket cost after aid? If language improvement is a goal, choose a program that guarantees a language course and a homestay. If clean, efficient credit transfer matters most, English-taught exchange destinations like Ireland are hard to beat.

Your application timeline

For a fall semester, go to your study abroad office's info sessions the previous September and October, shortlist programs by December, and apply between January and March. Summer programs move faster, with many deadlines in late winter. Providers often admit on a rolling basis, but the best scholarships close early, so apply for funding first and programs second.

Finally, check your passport's expiry and start visa paperwork at least four months out, since some destinations take that long. With a clear route chosen and funding lined up, the process stops feeling overwhelming and starts feeling like a plan.

faq.a: Yes. Pell Grants and Stafford loans apply to approved, credit-bearing programs through your home university. Confirm the program is approved before you enroll.

faq.q: Which providers are best for study abroad in Europe?
faq.a: CIEE, SIT, API Abroad and IES Abroad all run large European portfolios. The best fit depends on your city, budget and academic needs, so compare their support and housing options directly.

faq.q: When should I apply for a fall semester in Europe?
faq.a: Aim to apply between January and March, after attending your study abroad office's info sessions in the prior fall. Scholarship deadlines come earlier, so start those first.

posts.bodyHtml:
Europe remains the single most popular region for American study abroad, with well over half of all US students overseas choosing it every year, according to IIE's Open Doors report. The reasons are clear: world-class universities, a huge range of English-taught courses, cheap flights between countries, and program providers that make the whole process simple.

This guide compares the best study abroad programs in Europe for American students by destination, provider, cost, and how US financial aid applies, so you can pick a country that actually fits your degree and your budget.

Key takeaways

  • Ireland, the UK, Spain, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Denmark are the most popular choices, each with a distinct cost and credit profile.
  • University exchanges and ISEP partners are the cheapest route; providers like CIEE, SIT, API Abroad and IES Abroad add full support for a higher fee.
  • US federal aid, including Pell Grants and Stafford loans, travels with you on approved, credit-bearing programs.
  • Gilman, the Fund for Education Abroad and Boren all fund European study.
  • Germany and Ireland offer the best value per dollar for most American students.
  • Apply 8 to 12 months ahead, with scholarship deadlines falling even earlier.

Why American students choose Europe

Europe wins on practical and cultural grounds at once. Most destinations offer English-taught coursework even in non-English-speaking countries, so a language barrier rarely blocks your degree plan. The Schengen area makes weekend travel cheap and easy, which is a big part of the appeal for students who want to see more than one country. And because US universities send so many students there, the infrastructure, from advising and credit transfer to insurance and alumni networks, is the most mature of any region.

The best European destinations at a glance

  • Ireland: English-speaking, genuinely welcoming to US students, and with fees comparable to a home semester; see the study in Ireland guide.
  • UK: the largest English-speaking choice, with historic universities and strong provider coverage, but the most expensive; the UK guide breaks down the costs.
  • Spain: the top choice for language learning and homestays, with strong semester and summer options in cities like Madrid, Seville and Barcelona.
  • France: Paris and Lyon programs run through nearly every major provider, mixing English-taught courses with French language instruction.
  • Germany: low or no tuition, outstanding engineering and sciences, and generous stipends for research stays; start with the Germany guide.
  • Italy: art, architecture, and culinary programs with excellent provider support in Florence, Rome and beyond.
  • Netherlands and Denmark: fully English-taught university systems and efficient campuses, though living costs run higher.

Top providers and how they differ

On a university exchange you pay your home tuition and live like a local student, which is the most economical model. ISEP (isep.org) extends that idea through a fee-based membership that adds hundreds of partner universities. If your school has no partner in your dream city, provider programs fill the gap: CIEE, SIT, API Abroad and IES Abroad all run European portfolios that include housing, excursions, local staff and insurance. Provider fees run higher than exchange tuition, but many students consider the structure worth the money, and each provider publishes its own grants and early-booking discounts.

Costs and using US financial aid in Europe

Total costs vary more by country than many students expect. Ireland and Germany are the standout value choices: Irish universities are comparatively affordable and fully English-taught, while German public universities charge little or no tuition. The UK and Switzerland sit at the top end, with provider programs in London often exceeding $20,000 all-in for a semester. Wherever you go, your Pell Grant and Stafford loans travel with you as long as the program is approved for credit by your home school, so confirm that approval with your financial aid office before you enroll.

Scholarships for Europe-bound American students

Dedicated funding is plentiful. The Benjamin A. Gilman Scholarship pays up to $5,000, and more for critical languages or STEM, to Pell-eligible students. The Fund for Education Abroad awards up to $5,000, and Boren funds longer stays with a federal service commitment. For research-minded students, DAAD administers dozens of awards specifically for Americans in Germany. Apply to three or four awards in the same cycle rather than betting everything on one, and track the main deadlines in our scholarship list.

How to apply

Attend your study abroad office's fairs in the fall, shortlist by country and program type by December, and file applications between January and March for a fall start. Providers run rolling admissions, but competitive scholarships close early, so begin the funding applications first. Check your passport now and leave three to four months for a visa if your destination requires one. A semester in Europe is a big decision, but the application itself is surprisingly mechanical once you have picked your country and your route.

posts.title: Paid Internships Abroad for US Students
posts.metaDescription: Paid internships abroad for US students: DAAD RISE, IAESTE, JET, the visa reality, working holidays, and how to apply for paid stipend programs.
posts.excerpt: Paid internships abroad for US students: the visa reality, paid research programs like DAAD RISE and IAESTE, paid teaching routes, and working holiday options.

faq.q: Can I legally do an internship abroad without a visa?
faq.a: Almost never. Most countries prohibit working on a tourist or short-stay Schengen visa. Choose programs like DAAD RISE or IAESTE that provide work authorization, or use a working holiday visa where available.

faq.q: Are international internships usually paid?
faq.a: No. Many placement providers place students in unpaid positions and charge a program fee. The paid routes are more likely to be government and research programs such as DAAD RISE, IAESTE and the JET Programme.

faq.q: Who can apply for DAAD RISE?
faq.a: Undergraduates from the US, Canada, the UK and Ireland in STEM or related fields, typically in their second, third or fourth year. Applications open in the fall for the following summer.

faq.q: Is teaching English abroad considered an internship?
faq.a: Not exactly, but programs like JET and Spain's auxiliar scheme offer paid, visa-sponsored work experience that many students use as their international internship.

faq.q: Which working holiday visas are open to US citizens?
faq.a: Ireland and New Zealand operate schemes for US citizens aged roughly 18 to 30 that allow full-time work. Canadian, British and Australian citizens have broader working holiday agreements with several countries.

posts.bodyHtml:
Paid internships abroad for US students exist, but they look different from the paid summer internships you might find at home. In most countries you cannot simply land in a city and start working: earning money requires legal work authorization, which is why the best-paid international internships come through structured programs that handle visas and stipends for you.

This guide covers the paid routes that genuinely work for American students, from research fellowships and government-run programs to reputable placement providers, plus the visa reality you need to understand before anything else.

Key takeaways

  • Working on a tourist visa is illegal nearly everywhere; choose programs that provide work authorization.
  • DAAD RISE pays US, Canadian, UK and Irish undergraduates for research internships in Germany.
  • IAESTE arranges STEM internships worldwide, usually with a stipend that covers living costs.
  • The JET Programme and Spain's auxiliar program are paid teaching routes that sponsor your visa.
  • Placement providers like CRCC Asia and The Intern Group often charge fees, and many placements are unpaid.
  • Working holiday visas in Ireland and New Zealand let US citizens earn money legally while they work.

The visa reality: you cannot just work abroad

The single biggest mistake students make is assuming a study abroad or tourist visa allows paid work. In the European Union, a short-stay Schengen visa explicitly forbids employment, and most countries only authorize paid internships through a formal sponsor. Instead of hunting for a random employer, target programs that come with work authorization built in, which is exactly what every paid program below provides.

Paid research internships

DAAD RISE in Germany

The DAAD RISE program (daad.de) places undergraduates from the US, Canada, the UK and Ireland in paid research internships at German universities and research institutes for 10 to 12 weeks each summer. You receive a stipend that covers living costs plus help finding accommodation, and applications open in the fall. Because German public universities charge no tuition, the entire experience is essentially funded. It is one of the most reliable paid international internships for STEM and science students, and our guide to studying in Germany for free explains the wider picture.

IAESTE

The IAESTE network (iaeste.org) organizes STEM internships in more than 80 countries through university-based committees. Placements usually pay enough to cover your living costs, and the organization handles much of the paperwork. Applications open early in the academic year, and many US schools have an IAESTE coordinator on campus, so ask at your career center.

Paid teaching and government programs

Several government-run programs pay salaries large enough to save money, sponsor visas, and still look outstanding on a resume. The JET Programme (jetprogramme.org) hires graduates, including Americans, to work in Japanese schools with a monthly salary around ¥280,000 and subsidized housing. Spain's North American Language and Culture Assistants program places US and Canadian citizens in schools for 12 to 16 hours a week in exchange for a modest monthly stipend. Both are technically teaching rather than internships, but they are the most realistic way for a new graduate to work abroad legally and get paid while doing it.

Placement providers: what they cost and whether to use them

Companies like CRCC Asia, The Intern Group, and the internship arms of CIEE and API Abroad sell structured placements in cities like London, Barcelona, Tokyo and Sydney. Be realistic about them: you pay a program fee, many placements are unpaid, and housing and visa support are added costs. Their real value is the network, the credit options, and the guaranteed experience if your home university awards credit. Ask three questions before paying: is the placement paid, is housing included, and does the fee cover visa help?

Working holidays and other legal ways to earn

For flexibility, look at working holiday visas. Ireland and New Zealand both run schemes open to US citizens aged roughly 18 to 30 that allow full-time work, while Canadian, British and Australian students have even broader working holiday agreements with several countries. These are not internships, but they let you fund an extended stay legally and build the same professional skills. US students still enrolled in a degree can also use the J-1 Summer Work Travel program through a designated sponsor.

How to apply and when to start

Start a full academic year ahead. DAAD RISE closes its application in December or January for the following summer; IAESTE and JET deadlines cluster in the fall and winter; and working holiday places are often released in waves. Treat the process like a job search: a tailored CV, a short cover letter, and one or two references. If funding is the concern, our scholarship list and the how to fund studies abroad guide cover the money side of going overseas.

posts.title: How to Study in Europe for Free
posts.focusKeyword: study abroad in Europe for free
posts.metaDescription: How to study abroad in Europe for free: the tuition-free exchange model, no-fee countries like Germany, closing scholarships, and hidden costs.
posts.excerpt: How to study abroad in Europe for free or nearly free: tuition-free exchange, no-fee destinations like Germany, closing scholarships, and the hidden costs to budget.
tags: study abroad in Europe for free

faq.q: Is it really possible to study abroad in Europe for free?
faq.a: Nearly. Exchanges let you pay your home tuition instead of foreign fees, and countries like Germany charge little or no tuition. With scholarships covering living costs, out-of-pocket costs can drop to a few thousand dollars.

faq.q: Which European countries charge no tuition?
faq.a: Germany is the standout for international students. Norway has historically charged none at public universities, though policy is reviewed periodically, and France and Austria keep public fees very low.

faq.q: Do US scholarships apply to European study abroad?
faq.a: Yes. Gilman (up to $5,000, more for critical languages or STEM), the Fund for Education Abroad (up to $5,000), Boren and DAAD all fund American students in Europe.

faq.q: What is a blocked account and do I need one?
faq.a: A blocked account (Sperrkonto) is a German visa requirement proving you have roughly 12,000 euros for your first year. The money is yours and is released in monthly instalments while you live there.

faq.q: Can I work part-time while studying in Europe?
faq.a: On most European student visas, yes, commonly up to 20 hours per week during term. This can cover food and transport, though it should not be your primary funding plan.

posts.bodyHtml:
Can an American student really study abroad in Europe for free? The honest answer is very nearly, if you choose the right model. Europe's public universities charge little or no tuition in several countries, and US exchange systems let you keep paying your normal home tuition while studying at a partner institution abroad. Combine those with targeted scholarships, and the out-of-pocket cost can drop to a few thousand dollars.

This guide explains the tuition-free exchange model, the cheapest destinations, the scholarships that close the gap, and the hidden costs you still need to plan for.

Key takeaways

  • Exchange programs let you pay home tuition instead of foreign fees, often the single biggest saving.
  • Germany, Norway and, for degree study, France offer no or very low tuition at public universities.
  • Gilman, the Fund for Education Abroad, Boren and DAAD all fund US students in Europe.
  • Living costs and the visa blocked-account requirement are the real bills; budget for both.
  • Part-time work up to 20 hours a week is allowed on many European student visas.
  • Plan 10 to 12 months ahead, because scholarship deadlines come first.

The tuition-free exchange model

Most US colleges have bilateral exchange partners in Europe. You pay your usual home tuition, the partner university charges nothing extra, and credit transfers like a normal semester. This instantly removes the biggest cost of study abroad. ISEP (isep.org) makes the model more flexible: for a membership fee, your university can place you in a network of hundreds of European partners. If your school has any exchange ties in Europe, start there before you look at anything else, because this is the closest thing to free that most students will ever find.

Low- and no-tuition destinations

Germany

Germany is the poster child: public universities charge no tuition for bachelor's and many master's programmes, even for international students, with only a semester contribution of roughly 200 to 400 euros. You must show funds, around 12,000 euros in a blocked account for the first year, but that money is yours and is released monthly. Our study in Germany for free guide covers the details. One exception to know: Baden-Wurttemberg charges moderate fees for non-EU students, so check your state.

Norway, France and Austria

Norway has historically charged no tuition at public universities, though the policy is periodically reviewed, so confirm the current rules before planning around it. France charges very low public university fees, and Austria keeps tuition minimal. For a semester exchange none of this matters, since you pay home tuition anyway, but if you are weighing a full degree, these countries change the math dramatically.

Scholarships that close the gap

Whatever the tuition, you still need flights, housing, food and insurance, typically $8,000 to $14,000 a semester. US students can cover much of that with scholarships. The Benjamin A. Gilman Scholarship (gilmanscholarship.org) pays up to $5,000 for Pell-eligible students, the Fund for Education Abroad grants up to $5,000, Boren funds longer stays with a service requirement, and DAAD offers German-specific awards. Your home university's study abroad office almost certainly holds smaller exchange grants as well, so ask before paying anything out of pocket. Start with our scholarship list.

Slashing living costs

Living costs, not tuition, are where most of the money goes. Choose exchange student housing or a shared flat rather than provider apartments, which can cost two to three times as much. Cook at home, shop at discount supermarkets, and use the student transport pass most European universities include in their semester fee. If your visa allows it, part-time work up to 20 hours a week can cover groceries and nights out, and student discounts apply to museums, rail passes and even flights across the EU.

The hidden costs nobody warns you about

Budget for the things that sneak up on first-timers: a student visa fee, mandatory health insurance that some countries require before you can enroll, a passport that may need renewing, and the phone plan you will switch to. Weekend travel is a real line item too, so decide how much of it you actually need. The without a full scholarship guide walks through realistic ways to cover these costs without relying on loans.

Build your plan and start early

Start ten to twelve months before you want to leave. Attend your study abroad office's info sessions, pick your exchange partner or provider by the winter, and file scholarship applications in their spring and fall cycles. Confirm with your financial aid office that your Pell Grant and loans still apply, then apply for your visa the moment you have your admission letter. Follow these steps, and "free" becomes "funded", which is the version that actually happens in practice.

posts.title: Study Abroad Scholarships for US Students
posts.focusKeyword: study abroad scholarships for US students
posts.metaDescription: Study abroad scholarships for US students: the full list from Gilman, the Fund for Education Abroad, Boren, Fulbright, plus provider and university grants.
posts.excerpt: The full list of study abroad scholarships for US students: federal awards like Gilman and Boren, nonprofit grants, provider funding, and how to stack them.

faq.q: What is the easiest study abroad scholarship to win?
faq.a: The Benjamin A. Gilman Scholarship for Pell-eligible students is the most accessible major award, because so many eligible students never apply. Provider and university grants are also comparatively winnable.

faq.q: Can I combine multiple study abroad scholarships?
faq.a: Yes. Gilman, the Fund for Education Abroad, provider grants and university awards can often be stacked. Apply to several in the same cycle and let your study abroad office help coordinate them.

faq.q: Do I need a Pell Grant to apply for Gilman?
faq.a: Yes. The Gilman Scholarship is for US undergraduates who currently receive a Federal Pell Grant and study abroad through a program approved by their home university.

faq.q: Are there scholarships for studying a language abroad?
faq.a: Yes. Boren funds critical-language study with a federal service commitment, and the Critical Language Scholarship pays for full-time summer language study at no cost to the student.

faq.q: What scholarships exist for Canadian, British and Australian students?
faq.a: Canadians should check their university's exchange awards and provincial loan programs, British students can apply to the UK's Turing Scheme, and Australians can use OS-HELP loans for overseas study.

posts.bodyHtml:
Money is the number one reason US students skip study abroad, which is a shame, because the dedicated study abroad scholarships for US students are far more generous than most people realize. Federal awards, nonprofit grants and provider-specific money exist precisely so that cost does not decide who goes abroad, and Pell-eligible students in particular have some of the best-funded options in the world.

This is the full list worth knowing in 2026: who funds what, who qualifies, how much, and how to stack the awards together.

Key takeaways

  • The Benjamin A. Gilman Scholarship is the big one: up to $5,000, or $8,000 for critical languages or STEM, for Pell Grant recipients.
  • Boren Awards fund up to $25,000 for critical-language study in exchange for federal service.
  • The Fund for Education Abroad gives up to $5,000, prioritizing underrepresented students.
  • Fulbright US Student grants fund a year abroad after graduation, and CLS pays for summer language study.
  • Providers such as CIEE, SIT, API and IES, plus most universities, run their own study abroad grants.
  • Your Pell Grant and federal loans travel with you on approved programs, money you are already entitled to.

Federal scholarships for study abroad

Benjamin A. Gilman International Scholarship

If you receive a Pell Grant, Gilman (gilmanscholarship.org) is the single most important award you can apply for. It pays up to $5,000 for a semester or summer program and up to $8,000 when you study a critical language or major in STEM.
