It is a federal program for US undergraduates, applications open twice a year, and the success rate is far better than for most named scholarships, simply because so many eligible students never apply.

Boren Awards

Boren (borenawards.org) funds study abroad tied to critical languages and national security priorities, with undergraduate scholarships up to $25,000. Recipients commit to working in the federal government for a year after graduation. It is competitive, but for students learning Arabic, Chinese, Russian, Portuguese or similar languages, it is the most generous US award available.

Fulbright US Student Program and CLS

For graduating seniors and recent graduates, the Fulbright US Student Program (usstudentprograms.org) funds a year of research or English teaching abroad, with deadlines typically in early October. The Critical Language Scholarship (clscholarship.org) covers an intensive summer of language study in a critical language, fully funded and with no service requirement.

Nonprofit and foundation awards

The Fund for Education Abroad (fundforeducationabroad.org) awards up to $5,000 with a strong commitment to students from underrepresented backgrounds, and it runs special grants including the Rainbow Scholarship for LGBTQ+ students. Phi Kappa Phi offers smaller study abroad grants to its members. Rather than browsing random scholarship databases, stick to vetted lists and the reputable names above, which have predictable deadlines and clear eligibility rules. Our scholarship list tracks the main cycles.

Provider and university scholarships

Every major provider runs its own funding. CIEE, SIT, API Abroad and IES Abroad all publish grant programs, often $500 to $2,000, and many offer early-booking discounts worth pursuing. Your own university is next: study abroad offices frequently hold small awards for students studying at partner institutions, and Honors colleges and academic departments have travel funds that go unclaimed every year. Ask directly rather than assuming nothing exists.

Use the federal aid you already have

Before hunting for new money, remember the money you already qualify for. Federal Pell Grants and Stafford loans apply to approved, credit-bearing study abroad programs, so the rules treat studying abroad almost like a semester on campus. A single conversation with your financial aid office can unlock several thousand dollars you were not counting on. The fund your studies abroad guide explains how to combine aid, grants and savings into one workable plan.

For Canadian, British and Australian students

Most of the awards above are for US citizens, but the equivalent options exist elsewhere. Canadian students should check their university's exchange scholarships and provincial loan programs, which often follow approved study abroad. British students can apply to the UK's Turing Scheme, which funds study and work periods abroad. Australian students can draw on OS-HELP loans for overseas study. Our study abroad hub points students of every nationality to the right starting place.

How to apply and stack awards

Apply early and apply to several: Gilman, the Fund for Education Abroad and your university's grant are usually combinable, and each uses essays that take time to polish. File federal and nonprofit applications in their fall and spring cycles, and provider applications as soon as they open. In practice, a Pell-eligible student can assemble $8,000 to $13,000 from Gilman, FEA and provider grants on top of existing aid, enough to cover most of a European semester.

posts.title: Summer Study Abroad With College Credit
posts.metaDescription: Summer study abroad programs that earn college credit: the three program types, top providers, how credit transfers, real costs, and how to fund them.
posts.excerpt: Summer study abroad programs that earn college credit: the three program types, top providers, how credit transfers, real costs, and how to fund a summer term.

faq.q: Do summer study abroad programs give college credit?
faq.a: Yes. Most award 3 to 9 US credits. Get the syllabus pre-approved by your study abroad office and registrar to guarantee the credit transfers to your degree.

faq.q: How much do summer programs cost?
faq.a: Typically $3,000 to $8,000 including tuition, housing and excursions, with flights and food on top. Federal aid, Gilman and provider grants can cover much of this.

faq.q: Can I use federal financial aid in the summer?
faq.a: Yes, if the program is approved for credit by your home university and you remain enrolled in the required number of credits for the summer term.

faq.q: Which providers are best for summer study abroad?
faq.a: CIEE, SIT, API Abroad, IES Abroad and Cultural Experiences Abroad all run large summer portfolios. Choose by destination, academic focus and housing style rather than brand alone.

faq.q: When should I apply for next summer?
faq.a: Research in October and November, confirm credit transfer by December, apply for scholarships in their winter cycles, and submit your program application by February or March.

posts.bodyHtml:
Summer study abroad programs are the fastest-growing corner of international education and the easiest to fit into a US degree. Instead of giving up a semester, you spend three to eight weeks abroad, usually earn transferable college credit, and return in time for fall classes. Because they are shorter, they cost a fraction of a full term and are open to students who cannot leave campus for an entire semester.

Here is how summer programs work, how credit transfers, what they really cost, and the funding that can cover them.

Key takeaways

  • Summer programs run 3 to 8 weeks and typically award 3 to 9 US college credits.
  • Three types exist: faculty-led, provider-run, and direct enrollment at a foreign university.
  • Credit transfers through pre-approval from your home study abroad office, so arrange it before you go.
  • Costs typically range from about $3,000 to $8,000 including tuition, housing and excursions.
  • Federal aid, Gilman summer cycles and provider grants all apply to summer study abroad.
  • Apply by late winter for the following summer; scholarships close even earlier.

Why summer study abroad works

The biggest advantage is structural. A summer term does not delay your degree, so it works for students in rigid majors, student athletes, and anyone balancing work or internships. It is also a natural first trip: shorter programs have lighter language requirements, smaller group sizes and more hand-holding. And because federal aid and scholarships apply, many students fund a summer abroad almost entirely with money they would have used on campus anyway.

The range of destinations is also wider than for a full semester. Summer terms run in big capital cities, small coastal towns, and everything in between, and because they are short, you can even pair two programs back to back in different countries in a single summer. Many students treat a summer course as the trial run for a longer exchange later, and study abroad offices usually welcome it as satisfying first-time-abroad requirements.

The three types of summer programs

Faculty-led programs

Your own department or university runs a 2-to-6-week course with a professor you already know. Credit transfers cleanly, the group travels together, and the price is the lowest of the three routes. This is where most first-time study abroad students start, and it doubles as a chance to build a real relationship with a faculty mentor.

Provider programs

CIEE, SIT Study Abroad, API Abroad, IES Abroad and Cultural Experiences Abroad all run summer terms in dozens of countries, from language and culture courses to environmental science and global health. You get housing, excursions, on-site staff and a transcript that usually transfers. Expect fees in the $4,000 to $8,000 range for 4 to 6 weeks.

Direct enrollment

Many European and Asian universities run international summer schools you can join directly. German public universities keep summer fees very low, which fits neatly with our guide to studying in Germany for free. You handle the logistics yourself, but the tuition is often the cheapest of all three routes.

How college credit transfers

Never assume the credit will transfer. Get the syllabus approved by your home study abroad office and registrar before you pay a deposit, and request a detailed transcript from the provider or host university. Most summer courses convert to 3 to 9 US credits depending on contact hours, and a pre-approved course keeps your scholarship and aid eligibility intact.

Costs and how to fund them

A typical summer program runs $3,000 to $8,000 including tuition, housing and excursions, with flights and food on top. Provider fees are usually all-inclusive, bundling tuition, housing, some meals, excursions and insurance, so compare them against a faculty-led trip where you may pay for flights and activities separately. Federal aid can apply when you enroll in the required number of summer credits. Pell-eligible students can use Gilman's summer cycles, and the Fund for Education Abroad plus provider grants, including early-booking discounts, cover much of the gap. Stacking two or three awards is common; our scholarship list tracks the deadlines.

Application timeline for next summer

Work backwards: research programs in October and November, confirm credit transfer before Christmas, and file scholarship applications in their winter cycles. Apply to the program itself by February or March; providers with rolling admissions usually confirm quickly. Book flights once you are accepted, and start visa paperwork immediately for destinations that need one, since summer embassy slots fill up fast. If you want a head start on the money side, our funding guide covers every strategy that works for shorter programs.

posts.title: Teach English Abroad: TEFL Guide & Destinations
posts.metaDescription: Teach English abroad: TEFL vs CELTA, requirements and costs, the best-paying destinations, and visa rules for US, Canadian, British and Australian grads.
posts.excerpt: Teach English abroad after graduation: TEFL vs CELTA, costs, the best-paying destinations, and the visa rules for US, Canadian, British and Australian citizens.

faq.q: Do I need a degree to teach English abroad?
faq.a: In almost every country, yes, a four-year bachelor's degree is the standard requirement for a legal work visa. The degree subject rarely matters.

faq.q: What is the difference between TEFL, TESOL and CELTA?
faq.a: TEFL and TESOL are general certificates, and a 120-hour online course is the common baseline. CELTA is a more rigorous, widely recognized qualification that serious employers and competitive markets prefer.

faq.q: Which country pays the most for teaching English?
faq.a: China typically offers the highest salaries, with Japan, South Korea and parts of the Middle East close behind. Europe, especially Spain, pays less but offers unmatched travel access.

faq.q: Do I need a TEFL certificate before applying to JET or EPIK?
faq.a: No. Government programs like JET and EPIK do not require TEFL, but having one makes you more competitive for other jobs and for the destinations that do require it.

faq.q: Is teaching English abroad worth the cost of getting certified?
faq.a: Yes. A $400 online TEFL pays for itself quickly, and a $2,000 CELTA opens better-paying, longer-term positions in markets that require recognized qualifications.

posts.bodyHtml:
Teaching English abroad is one of the few jobs you can land straight out of university with no prior experience, and demand remains strong across Asia, Europe, the Middle East and Latin America. For American, Canadian, British and Australian graduates, it is a realistic way to live overseas for a year or two, build savings in some destinations, and return with a genuinely international CV, or simply stay longer than you planned.

This guide covers the requirements, the certificates and what they cost, the destinations that actually pay well, and the visa reality behind every teaching job.

Key takeaways

  • You need a bachelor's degree and native-level English; most employers want a TEFL or TESOL certificate too.
  • A 120-hour online TEFL course ($300 to $600) is enough for many jobs; CELTA ($1,500 to $2,500) matters most for career teachers.
  • The JET Programme in Japan and Spain's auxiliar program are the most popular sponsored routes for Western graduates.
  • Salaries range from enough to break even (Spain) to genuine savings (Japan, South Korea, China, parts of Vietnam).
  • Employers must sponsor your work visa; working on a tourist visa is illegal everywhere.
  • Plan six to twelve months ahead, including background checks and authenticated documents.

The basic requirements

The universal baseline is a four-year bachelor's degree and native-level English; employers usually verify this with a passport or an interview rather than a test. Beyond that, a TEFL certificate is expected almost everywhere, and a clean criminal background check is required in most countries. Many governments also require documents such as apostilled degree certificates, so start gathering paperwork early. Age limits, teaching experience and accent preferences vary by destination, so check each program's fine print.

TEFL, TESOL or CELTA: what to choose

The certificate you need depends on where you want to teach. A 120-hour TEFL or TESOL course from a reputable provider, usually $300 to $600 online, satisfies employers across Asia, Latin America and the Middle East. If you want a career in teaching or a position in a competitive European market, a CELTA (or Trinity CertTESOL) is the gold standard: an intensive four-week course costing roughly $1,500 to $2,500 that serious employers and government programs accept and often require. Choose the destination first, because your destination decides your certificate.

Best destinations and what they pay

  • Japan (JET Programme): a monthly salary around 280,000 yen, subsidized housing, and visa sponsorship; applications open in the fall through jetprogramme.org.
  • Spain (auxiliar program): US and Canadian citizens teach 12 to 16 hours a week for a modest monthly stipend, enough to live on in many regions, with excellent travel access.
  • South Korea (EPIK): paid accommodation and strong salaries for new and experienced teachers alike.
  • China: the highest salaries in the industry, though program choice matters more than ever; teach only for accredited, vetted schools.
  • Vietnam and Thailand: lower salaries but very low living costs, great for breaking even while enjoying Southeast Asia.
  • Czech Republic and the UAE: interesting options for certified teachers, though entry requirements are higher.

Visas, contracts and legalities

Legality is non-negotiable: a work visa, not a tourist visa, is required to teach, and schools that offer to "sort it out later" should be avoided. The safest routes are government programs like JET, EPIK and Spain's auxiliares, because they handle sponsorship, health care and contracts properly. For direct jobs, ask for the contract in writing, check the employer's accreditation, and never pay a recruiter before verifying the school. British, Canadian and Australian citizens also have working holiday visas with several countries that make moving abroad much simpler.

How much it costs to get started

Getting ready costs less than most people think: roughly $400 to $700 for an online TEFL, or $1,500 to $2,500 for CELTA, plus around $1,000 to $2,000 for flights and a startup buffer. Most reputable employers provide or help with housing, and government programs cover or subsidize accommodation. Teaching abroad is genuinely a net-positive money move in destinations like Japan, Korea and China, and a break-even adventure in Europe.

Making it count

The best teaching jobs abroad double as career moves: CELTA graduates can move into international school teaching, and a year in the classroom is excellent preparation for fields like education, TESOL graduate study, diplomacy and development. Pair the income with good savings habits, and you come home with more than a paycheck. Our study abroad hub has more on structuring a longer time overseas, the study in Spain guide covers one of the most popular placements, and the scholarship list is useful if you combine teaching with further study.

posts.title: How Much Does Studying Abroad Cost? 2026 Budget Guide
posts.metaDescription: How much does studying abroad cost in 2026? Real tuition, living costs and visa fees for 12 countries, plus a step-by-step budget builder.
posts.excerpt: Real 2026 study abroad costs by country, including tuition, living expenses and visa fees, plus a budget builder that shows exactly where the money goes.

faq.q: How much does it really cost to study abroad in 2026?
faq.a: It depends almost entirely on destination. A year in Germany, Italy or Spain can cost €12,000–18,000 all-in, while a year in Australia runs AUD 70,000–95,000 and a private US college can pass $85,000. Always add visa fees, insurance and a 10% buffer on top of tuition and living costs.

faq.q: Which country is the cheapest to study abroad in 2026?
faq.a: Turkey is the cheapest overall (public tuition US$600–4,000 plus living costs of US$3,000–6,000 a year), followed by Germany, where most public universities charge no tuition and the €11,904 blocked-account proof of funds is your realistic annual budget.

faq.q: What hidden costs should I budget for?
faq.a: Visa fees (AUD 2,500 in Australia, £558 plus £776/year IHS in the UK, $535 in the US), mandatory health insurance, a renewed passport, phone plans, residence permits and weekend travel. A 10% buffer covers most of these; nearly every student uses it.

faq.q: Can I study abroad without paying full price?
faq.a: Yes. Exchange programs let you pay home tuition, public universities in Germany, Italy, Spain and Turkey charge little or nothing, and scholarships like Gilman ($5,000), the Fund for Education Abroad and Boren, plus federal aid, routinely cover $5,000–10,000 of the cost.

faq.q: How much money do I need to show for a student visa?
faq.a: Typical 2026 benchmarks are €11,904 for Germany, CAD 20,635 for Canada, AUD 29,710 for Australia and NZD 20,000 for New Zealand, plus proof of first-year tuition, return travel and insurance. Countries use these figures to assess whether you can support yourself.

posts.bodyHtml:
The honest answer to how much study abroad cost in 2026 is that it depends more on your destination than on any other single factor. A year at a German public university can run roughly €12,000–15,000 all-in because tuition is free, while a year at a private US college can pass $85,000. The gap between the cheapest and most expensive countries is a factor of five or more, so the single most important budgeting decision you make is where you go. This guide breaks down the real cost of studying abroad in 2026, country by country, and shows you how to build a budget you can actually stick to.

Before you panic at a price tag, remember that the sticker number is never the whole story. Scholarships, cheaper cities, public universities and part-time work routinely cut thousands off the bill, and some of the world's best universities are among the cheapest to attend. Understanding where the money goes is the difference between a year abroad and a debt hangover.

Key takeaways

  • Four costs dominate every budget: tuition or program fees, housing, flights, and daily living.
  • The country choice matters more than anything else, with an all-in range from roughly €12,000 (Germany) to over $85,000 (private US colleges).
  • Government-run visa, health and immigration charges are bigger than most students expect, e.g. Australia's AUD 2,500 student visa fee.
  • Exchange programs (paying home tuition) usually beat provider programs by $3,000 to $8,000 a semester.
  • Gilman, the Fund for Education Abroad, Boren and your federal aid can cover $5,000 to $10,000 before you touch a loan.
  • A 10% buffer plus a written budget is the cheapest insurance you can buy.

How much does studying abroad cost in 2026?

In round numbers, a full year of study abroad in 2026 runs roughly:

  • US$25,000–50,000 for a year at a public US university (out-of-state), $50,000–95,000 at a top private one.
  • £30,000–45,000 for a year in the UK, where tuition is £25,000–45,000 and London living costs around £1,529 a month.
  • CAD 40,000–60,000 for a year in Canada, where tuition runs CAD 20,000–50,000 and living costs are set at CAD 20,635 a year.
  • AUD 70,000–95,000 for a year in Australia, the most expensive option, with tuition AUD 35,000–42,000 and a living-cost benchmark of AUD 29,710.
  • €12,000–18,000 for a year in Germany, Italy or Spain, the value picks of Western Europe.
  • €20,000–30,000 for a year in the Netherlands, France or Ireland, where tuition is moderate but living costs are high.
  • US$5,000–12,000 for a year in Turkey, where public tuition runs US$600–4,000 and living costs around US$3,000–6,000.

The four costs that make up your total

Every budget breaks into the same four buckets, and each needs its own plan.

1. Tuition and program fees

This is usually the largest line item and the one most shaped by your route. In Germany, most public universities charge no tuition, just a semester fee of €300–350; in the US, out-of-state public tuition runs $30,000–55,000 and private colleges $65,000–70,000+. Our guide to studying in Germany for free and the free study in Europe guide show the mechanics of the tuition-free routes.

2. Housing

Housing is the second biggest cost and the most variable by city. Budget £700–1,500 a month in London, $1,000–2,400 in Amsterdam, €350–700 in Spanish student cities, and NZ$600–1,200 a month in Auckland or Wellington. University dorms are almost always cheaper than private rentals, and exchange housing is usually the cheapest option of all.

3. Flights

A return flight is a one-off, but it is easily $800–2,000 depending on route and booking date. Book three to four months out and fly midweek to keep it down.

4. Daily living

Food, transport, phone and entertainment quietly add $600–1,200 a month in most countries. Australia's official benchmark is AUD 29,710 a year, Canada sets living costs at CAD 20,635, and New Zealand uses NZD 20,000, which gives you a credible planning number even if real cities cost more.

Visa and hidden costs nobody warns you about

The sneaky costs are where budgets die. Australia's student visa fee jumped to AUD 2,500 from July 2026. The UK charges a £558 visa plus the Immigration Health Surcharge at £776 a year, which alone is £2,716 for a three-year degree. The US adds a $350 SEVIS fee and a $185 MRV fee, a mandatory $535 before you file. Add mandatory health insurance (AUD 500–1,000 in Australia, €120–250 a month in the Netherlands), a renewed passport, a local phone plan, and weekend travel, and you can see where the 10% buffer goes.

How to pay for studying abroad

The smartest order of operations is to use federal aid first, since Pell Grants and Stafford loans follow you to approved programs, then stack scholarships like Gilman (up to $5,000), the Fund for Education Abroad and Boren Awards, and finally fill any gap with savings or a part-time job before you leave. Our study abroad scholarships guide and the how to fund study abroad guide cover the full list, and many students assemble $5,000–10,000 in aid and grants without touching a loan.

Build your own budget in six steps

  1. Write down your program fee or home tuition for the full period.
  2. Add housing for every month, using the country's official living-cost benchmark as your floor.
  3. Add return flights, visa fees, health insurance and a phone plan.
  4. Estimate daily living at the country's realistic rate, not the optimistic one.
  5. Add a 10% buffer, then subtract the aid, scholarships and savings you can count on.
  6. The remainder is the honest number you need to raise, so keep it somewhere you will actually check.

Be honest about exchange rates too. Prices in euros, pounds or yen fluctuate, so plan around a conservative conversion rather than the rate you see on the day you book. Students who do this math in writing report fewer surprises, which is exactly what a year abroad should be.

The moves that save thousands

Choose a public university in a lower-cost country (Germany, Italy, Spain and Turkey lead the pack), take exchange housing over a provider apartment, book flights early, cook most meals, and use student discounts religiously. Studying in the country directly rather than through a provider program routinely saves $3,000–8,000 a semester. And never pay sticker price: apply to scholarships even if you think you will not win, because the same essays you write for admissions double as scholarship applications. Start with our guide to scholarships you are actually eligible for.

For a region-by-region breakdown of programs, housing and funding, see our study abroad programs guide and the full scholarship list.

posts.title: Commonwealth Scholarship: Complete UK Guide
posts.metaDescription: Commonwealth Scholarship guide: eligibility, funding, what it covers, and how to apply through your country's nominating agency for fully funded UK study.
posts.excerpt: Everything you need to know about the Commonwealth Scholarship: who qualifies, what it covers, how to apply through your nominating agency, and key deadlines.

faq.q: Is the Commonwealth Scholarship fully funded?
faq.a: Yes. The award typically covers full tuition fees, a monthly living stipend, return airfare, and additional allowances such as a warm clothing allowance, study travel grant, and thesis grant for doctoral scholars. Exact amounts are reviewed each cycle.

faq.q: Can I apply directly to the Commonwealth Scholarship Commission?
faq.a: No. For most awards you must first be nominated by your country's designated nominating agency or apply through a UK university, depending on the award type. The CSC does not accept direct applications.

faq.q: Which countries are eligible for the Commonwealth Scholarship?
faq.a: Eligibility is limited to citizens of Commonwealth countries, with the exact list depending on the award and reviewed annually. Check the current list of eligible countries on the CSC website before applying.

faq.q: What is the application deadline for the Commonwealth Scholarship?
faq.a: Applications typically open in September and close in mid to late October for study starting the following autumn. Nominating agency deadlines are usually several weeks earlier, so confirm your national deadline first.

faq.q: Can I apply with a lower second-class degree?
faq.a: A 2:2 can be accepted if it is combined with a relevant postgraduate qualification such as a master's degree. On its own, a 2:2 is unlikely to be competitive.

posts.bodyHtml:
The Commonwealth Scholarship is the UK government's flagship funding scheme for postgraduate students from Commonwealth countries, offering a fully funded place at a UK university. It is administered by the Commonwealth Scholarship Commission (CSC) on behalf of the UK government and has supported generations of future leaders for more than six decades. For eligible applicants it covers tuition, a monthly stipend, return airfare, and a range of allowances, which makes it one of the most generous routes to studying in the UK.

This guide explains what the Commonwealth Scholarship is, who qualifies, what it covers, and how the application process actually works. Understand one detail first: the CSC does not accept direct applications, so the route through your country's nominating agency is essential.

Key takeaways

  • The Commonwealth Scholarship is fully funded, covering tuition, a monthly living stipend, return airfare, and additional allowances.
  • It is open to citizens of eligible Commonwealth countries who are permanently resident there and cannot otherwise afford UK study.
  • You apply through a national nominating agency or a UK university, not directly to the CSC.
  • Master's awards fund one year of study; PhD awards fund up to 36 months of doctoral research.
  • Applications typically open in September and close in October, with nominating agency deadlines falling even earlier.

What is the Commonwealth Scholarship?

The Commonwealth Scholarship and Fellowship Plan is one of the world's oldest international scholarship programmes. Each year the CSC funds hundreds of scholars to complete master's or doctoral degrees at UK universities.

The programme's purpose is explicitly developmental: scholars are expected to return to their home countries and apply what they have learned, and this mission shapes the eligibility rules and the way panels assess your plans.

Who can apply: eligibility essentials

Eligibility is strict, and the list of eligible countries is reviewed each year, so always confirm your status on the official CSC website (cscuk.fcdo.gov.uk) before investing time in an application. In general, applicants must:

  • Be a citizen of (or hold refugee status in) an eligible Commonwealth country and be permanently resident there.
  • Hold a first degree of at least upper second-class (2:1) honours standard, or a lower second-class degree plus a relevant postgraduate qualification.
  • Be unable to afford to study in the UK without the scholarship.
  • Not have studied or worked for one academic year or more in a high-income country.
  • Be available to start study in the UK in September or October of the award year.

What does the Commonwealth Scholarship cover?

While specific figures are reviewed each cycle, a Commonwealth Scholarship typically covers full tuition fees, a monthly living stipend (higher in the London area), return economy airfare, and a warm clothing allowance where relevant. Doctoral scholars also receive a thesis grant and most a study travel grant.

The award is designed to be comprehensive, so if you are selected you can live and study in the UK without funding your own tuition or basic living costs. If you are still mapping your options, start with our guide to finding scholarships you are actually eligible for, or browse the full range on our scholarship results page.

The main award types

Commonwealth Master's Scholarships

Commonwealth Master's Scholarships fund a one-year taught master's degree at an eligible UK university. They are open to candidates from low and middle income Commonwealth countries, with selection weighing academic merit and the likely development impact on your home country.

Commonwealth PhD Scholarships

Commonwealth PhD Scholarships fund up to 36 months of doctoral research at a UK university. Separate competitions exist for candidates from least developed and fragile states and for candidates from high income countries, so check which one applies to you.

Commonwealth Shared Scholarships

Commonwealth Shared Scholarships are jointly funded by the CSC and UK universities and are tied to a published list of eligible master's courses. Because you apply directly to the CSC rather than through a nominating agency, they are a useful second route if your course is on the list.

How to apply step by step

Step 1: Confirm eligibility

Start at cscuk.fcdo.gov.uk to confirm your country is eligible and identify your nominating agency, usually a government ministry, commission, or designated body.

Step 2: Apply to your nominating agency

The nominating agency runs its own competition with an internal deadline several weeks before the CSC deadline; only nominated candidates proceed, so follow its instructions exactly.

Step 3: Prepare your supporting documents

You will typically need your passport, transcripts and certificates, two references, and a personal statement explaining your development goals and how UK study helps you achieve them.

Step 4: Complete the CSC application

If your nominating agency selects you, complete the formal application through the CSC's online system before the closing date.

Step 5: Wait for selection

Panels assess academic merit, your study plan, and the likely impact on your country; successful candidates are notified in the months before the year begins.

Key dates and timeline

Applications for the Commonwealth Scholarship typically open in September and close in mid to late October for study starting the following autumn. Shared Scholarship deadlines often fall later, around December. Because nominating agency deadlines come earlier, you should begin preparing in the summer at the latest, and always confirm exact dates on the CSC website for your specific award.

If you are also considering the UK's other flagship award, read our guide to the Chevening Scholarship and compare the two carefully, since the eligibility rules and application routes are very different.

Tips to strengthen your application

  • Start with the nominating agency deadline, not the CSC deadline, and work backwards.
  • Make your personal statement specific about the development problems you want to address and how this exact degree will help.
  • Secure a UK university offer early where your award type allows it; a strong admission letter strengthens your case.
  • Apply the framework from our guide to building a competitive scholarship profile to present a coherent story.
  • Read the full eligibility criteria and follow every formatting instruction, since compliance is an easy first filter.

posts.title: Rhodes Scholarship: How to Apply to Oxford
posts.metaDescription: Rhodes Scholarship guide: eligibility, what it covers, selection criteria, and how to apply through your constituency for fully funded study at Oxford.
posts.excerpt: Learn how the Rhodes Scholarship works, what it covers at Oxford, who qualifies, and how to build a competitive application before your constituency deadline.

faq.q: What does the Rhodes Scholarship cover?
faq.a: The award typically covers Oxford university and college fees, a living stipend, return economy airfare, the student visa fee and Immigration Health Surcharge, and a settling-in allowance. Exact figures are reviewed annually.

faq.q: Is there an age limit for the Rhodes Scholarship?
faq.a: Most constituencies require applicants to be between 19 and 25 years old at the time of application, though the exact range can differ by region. Check your constituency's rules on the official website.

faq.q: Do I apply directly to Oxford for the Rhodes Scholarship?
faq.a: No. You apply through your Rhodes constituency first. If selected, you then apply separately to the University of Oxford for admission to your chosen course.

faq.q: Can I apply for the Rhodes Scholarship more than once?
faq.a: You can apply a maximum of two times in your lifetime to the same constituency. Because of this limit, it is worth preparing thoroughly before your first attempt.

faq.q: Are international students eligible for the Rhodes Scholarship?
faq.a: Yes, if you are a citizen of an eligible Rhodes constituency. The constituencies cover most countries, and each has its own eligibility criteria, so verify yours on rhodesscholar.org.

posts.bodyHtml:
The Rhodes Scholarship is one of the oldest and most prestigious scholarships in the world, funding outstanding young people from around the globe to study any full-time postgraduate degree at the University of Oxford. Founded through the will of Cecil Rhodes, the scholarship has supported more than 8,000 scholars who have gone on to lead in every field. Winning a Rhodes Scholarship means more than free tuition; it means joining a global community built to develop future leaders.

This guide explains how the Rhodes Scholarship works, who can apply, what it covers, how selection happens, and how to build a strong application. Understand one structural fact first: the scholarship is organised into constituencies, usually by country or region, and each one runs its own selection process with its own deadline.

Key takeaways

  • The Rhodes Scholarship funds any full-time postgraduate degree at the University of Oxford, from master's courses to a DPhil.
  • It covers university and college fees, a generous living stipend, and travel costs, making study at Oxford essentially free.
  • Applications are made through regional constituencies, each with its own eligibility rules and deadline.
  • You can apply to the Rhodes Scholarship a maximum of two times in your lifetime.
  • Winning the scholarship does not guarantee admission to Oxford; admission is a separate process.

What is the Rhodes Scholarship?

The Rhodes Scholarship is a fully funded postgraduate award for study at the University of Oxford in the United Kingdom. Scholars may pursue any full-time postgraduate course Oxford offers, from one-year master's programmes to research degrees such as the DPhil, subject to the rules of their constituency.

The scholarship was founded to develop leaders who contribute to the common good, and it remains true to that mission: committees look beyond academic records to character, leadership, and commitment to making a difference.

Eligibility: which constituencies can apply

The Rhodes Scholarship is open to citizens of eligible countries and regions, known as constituencies, which together cover most of the world. Because rules vary, you must check the eligibility criteria for your specific constituency on the official website, rhodesscholar.org. Common requirements include:

  • Be a citizen of (or meet the residency rules for) an eligible Rhodes constituency.
  • Be aged within the range set by your constituency, which is commonly between 19 and 25.
  • Hold an undergraduate degree or be on track to complete one before taking up the scholarship.
  • Meet any academic minimum, which is typically set at a very high level of achievement.

US applicants apply through one of 16 regional districts and must first be endorsed by their university, a process whose internal deadline can fall months before the national one; Canadian and most other applicants apply through their country's dedicated constituency.

What does the Rhodes Scholarship cover?

While exact figures change each year, a Rhodes Scholarship typically covers the university and college fees for your chosen Oxford course, a generous annual living stipend for accommodation and day-to-day costs, and the return economy airfare between your home and the UK. The award also covers the student visa fee and the Immigration Health Surcharge, and a settling-in allowance when you arrive.

Stipend levels are reviewed annually, so verify current rates on the official website. For a wider view of funded UK options, browse our scholarship results page.

Selection criteria

The Rhodes Trust publishes the qualities it looks for, and committees weigh all of them:

  • Academic excellence, demonstrated through your record and referees' assessments.
  • Energy to use your talents to the full, and ambition to apply them beyond your degree.
  • Truth, courage, devotion to duty, and sympathy for the protection of the weak.
  • Leadership potential and an instinct to defend the common good.
  • Moral force of character and an interest in your fellow human beings.

Your personal statement, references, and interview are the evidence for these qualities, so the scholarship rewards candidates who can show depth, not just excellent grades.

How to apply step by step

Identify your constituency

Find your country's constituency on the Rhodes Trust website and read its instructions. US applicants should contact their university's fellowship office early, since campus endorsement deadlines can be months before the national deadline.

Gather your materials

Most constituencies require an online application with your academic record, a CV, a personal statement, and a statement of your study plans at Oxford; some ask for additional essays and photos, so follow the checklist for your constituency.

Secure your referees

You typically need five or more references. Choose people who know you well and can speak to your academic ability and your character, and give them time to write thoughtfully.

Submit and prepare for interviews

Shortlisted candidates are interviewed by their constituency's selection committee; successful candidates then apply to Oxford for admission.

Apply to Oxford

Selection as a Rhodes Scholar and admission to Oxford are separate decisions: the Trust supports your Oxford application, but your chosen course must still accept you.

Key dates and timeline

Rhodes applications typically open in June and close between July and October depending on the constituency. For many regions the deadline falls between late August and early October for entry the following year. The US national deadline is usually early October, with campus endorsement deadlines much earlier. Check the schedule for your constituency on rhodesscholar.org and start early, because you are limited to two lifetime applications.

Tips to stand out

  • Begin with your campus or national fellowship office, if you have one; they know the local process and deadlines.
  • Write a personal statement that shows who you are rather than re-listing achievements; our guide to writing a winning statement of purpose has transferable advice.
  • Choose referees who know you personally and can attest to character, not just grades; see how to get strong letters of recommendation.
  • Research your intended Oxford course in detail and show why it fits your plans; this is a common place where applications look generic.
  • Build your leadership record over time rather than at the last minute, drawing on our advice for a competitive scholarship profile.

posts.title: Gates Cambridge Scholarship: Fully Funded Guide
posts.metaDescription: Gates Cambridge Scholarship guide: eligibility, funding, application rounds and deadlines for fully funded study at Cambridge.
posts.excerpt: A complete guide to the Gates Cambridge Scholarship covering what it funds, who can apply, the two application rounds, and how to write the Gates essay.

faq.q: Is the Gates Cambridge Scholarship fully funded?
faq.a: Yes. It covers the full cost of postgraduate study at Cambridge, including the university composition fee, college fees, a maintenance allowance, airfare, and visa and Immigration Health Surcharge costs, plus an academic development fund.

faq.q: Who is eligible for the Gates Cambridge Scholarship?
faq.a: Citizens of any country outside the United Kingdom who are applying for an eligible full-time postgraduate course at Cambridge, such as a PhD, MPhil, MLitt, or one-year course. US citizens resident in the US apply in the earlier US round.

faq.q: What is the application deadline for the Gates Cambridge Scholarship?
faq.a: US citizens resident in the US must apply by a mid-October deadline. All other applicants face a December or early January deadline depending on their course. Confirm your course's deadline in the Cambridge course directory.

faq.q: Do I need a separate application for Gates Cambridge?
faq.a: No. You apply through the standard Cambridge graduate application portal and select Gates Cambridge as a funding option, completing the Gates-specific questions in the same form.

faq.q: How competitive is the Gates Cambridge Scholarship?
faq.a: Very competitive, with thousands of applicants competing for around 80 awards each year. A strong academic record, genuine leadership, and a specific commitment to improving lives are all essential.

posts.bodyHtml:
The Gates Cambridge Scholarship is one of the most prestigious fully funded awards for postgraduate study in the world, funding outstanding students from outside the United Kingdom to study at the University of Cambridge. Established in 2000 with a major endowment from the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, the programme awards around 80 full-cost scholarships each year to students pursuing a PhD, MPhil, MLitt, or one-year postgraduate course. Its mission is to build a global network of future leaders committed to improving the lives of others.

This guide explains what the Gates Cambridge Scholarship covers, who can apply, how the two application rounds work, and how to build an application that fits the programme's values. Because Gates Cambridge is part of the normal Cambridge graduate application, the mechanics are simpler than many applicants expect.

Key takeaways

  • The Gates Cambridge Scholarship is a full-cost award covering tuition, college fees, a maintenance allowance, airfare, and more.
  • It is open to students from any country outside the UK applying for a postgraduate degree at Cambridge, with around two-thirds of awards going to PhD students.
  • There are two rounds: an early one for US citizens resident in the US, and the main international round for everyone else.
  • You apply through Cambridge's graduate application portal and select Gates Cambridge as a funding option; there is no separate scholarship form.
  • Selection weighs academic ability, leadership, and a demonstrated commitment to improving the lives of others.

What is the Gates Cambridge Scholarship?

The Gates Cambridge Scholarship was founded to recognise and support academically outstanding students who also show strong leadership potential and a commitment to improving the lives of others. Scholars join a community of thousands of alumni and current scholars working across every field, from artificial intelligence and medicine to law, development, and the arts.

Because the award was established by the Gates Foundation with a distinctive mission, selection is holistic. You are assessed not only on whether you can succeed at Cambridge, but on whether you are the kind of person the programme was built to support.

Eligibility: who can apply

You can apply for a Gates Cambridge Scholarship if you are a citizen of any country outside the United Kingdom and you are applying for one of the eligible full-time postgraduate courses at Cambridge. The main eligible courses are the PhD, the MPhil, the MLitt, and one-year postgraduate courses. A small number of professional courses, such as an MBA or MFin, are not eligible.

Applicants must submit a complete application for admission to their chosen course through the Cambridge graduate application portal, including the Gates Cambridge section and its essay. US citizens who are resident in the United States must apply in the earlier US round.

What does the award cover?

Gates Cambridge is a full-cost award. It typically covers the university composition fee and college fees for your course, a maintenance allowance to cover living costs, the cost of a return airfare, and the costs of the visa and Immigration Health Surcharge. Scholars also receive a discretionary academic development fund that can support conference attendance, fieldwork, or other academic activities, and there is provision for family allowance in limited circumstances.

Exact amounts are set each year, so confirm the current package on the official website, gatescambridge.org, before you apply. For a wider view of funded UK options, see our scholarship results page.

The two application rounds

Gates Cambridge runs two application rounds each year.

US round

US citizens who are resident in the United States at the time of application apply in the US round, with a deadline in mid-October. Around a quarter of the annual awards are made in this round, and candidates receive decisions in late winter.

International round

All other eligible applicants apply in the international round, aligned with the university's funding competition. Deadlines fall in December or early January depending on your chosen course, with decisions announced in early spring.

Whichever round you apply in, the scholarship is part of your standard Cambridge application, so the main task is building an excellent postgraduate application.

How to apply step by step

Choose your course

Research Cambridge courses and check the application deadline for each one in the university's course directory. Your course deadline determines when you must submit.

Submit the graduate application

Complete the Cambridge online application for admission, including academic history, references, and supporting documents.

Complete the Gates Cambridge section

In the funding section of the application, select Gates Cambridge. You will answer questions including the Gates essay on your commitment to improving the lives of others, which is central to assessment.

Secure your references

You need references, at least one of which must be academic. They must be submitted by the application deadline, so brief your referees weeks in advance.

Submit before your deadline

Applications are submitted through the Cambridge portal by the deadline for your course and round. Late applications are not considered.

Key dates

For US citizens resident in the US, the deadline is typically mid-October. For all other applicants, deadlines fall in December or early January depending on the course, with applications opening around September. Interviews, where held, take place in late winter or early spring, and offers are made shortly afterwards. Always check the current dates on gatescambridge.org and the Cambridge course directory.

Tips for a strong application

  • Write the Gates essay about real commitments and concrete impact, not generic ambitions; it should be specific to your experiences.
  • Line up strong referees early, because late references can disqualify an otherwise complete application; use our guide to strong letters of recommendation.
  • Build your case for leadership with evidence, following our framework for a competitive scholarship profile.
  • Draft your personal statements and academic statement with the structure in our statement of purpose guide.
  • Explore other funded UK options so you have a plan if your Gates application is unsuccessful.

posts.title: Schwarzman Scholars: Fully Funded Master's in Beijing
posts.metaDescription: Schwarzman Scholars guide: fully funded one-year master's in Global Affairs at Tsinghua Beijing for emerging leaders, with eligibility and deadlines.
posts.excerpt: Everything you need to know about Schwarzman Scholars, including what the award covers, the age and English requirements, and how to apply.

faq.q: Is Schwarzman Scholars fully funded?
faq.a: Yes. The award covers tuition and fees, room and board, travel to and from Beijing, a laptop, health insurance, books and supplies, an in-country study tour, and a monthly personal stipend.

faq.q: What is the age limit for Schwarzman Scholars?
faq.a: You must be at least 18 but not yet 29 years old as of August 1 of your enrollment year. The rule is strict and applied consistently.

faq.q: Where do Schwarzman Scholars study?
faq.a: At Schwarzman College, Tsinghua University, in Beijing, China. All scholars pursue the one-year master's in Global Affairs, choosing a concentration in public policy, economics and business, or international studies.

faq.q: Do I need to speak Chinese to apply?
faq.a: No. The program is taught entirely in English, and Chinese language classes are optional. You do need to demonstrate strong English proficiency unless you studied in English.

faq.q: What is the Schwarzman Scholars deadline?
faq.a: For US and global applicants, the application typically opens in early spring and closes in early September for entry the following August. Chinese citizens follow an earlier timeline.

posts.bodyHtml:
The Schwarzman Scholars program is a prestigious, fully funded, one-year master's in Global Affairs at Tsinghua University in Beijing, China. Founded by businessman and philanthropist Stephen A. Schwarzman, the program was created to prepare the next generation of global leaders with a deep understanding of China in a changing world. Each year around 200 scholars from dozens of countries study together at Schwarzman College, one of the most selective graduate communities anywhere.

This guide explains how Schwarzman Scholars works, what the award covers, who can apply, and how to build a strong application. If you are an emerging leader who wants to combine graduate study in China with an intense leadership experience, this program deserves serious attention.

Key takeaways

  • Schwarzman Scholars is a fully funded one-year master's in Global Affairs at Tsinghua University in Beijing.
  • It covers tuition, room and board, travel to and from Beijing, a laptop, health insurance, and a monthly personal stipend.
  • Applicants must be at least 18 but not yet 29 as of August 1 of the enrollment year and hold a bachelor's degree.
  • The program is taught in English, with three academic concentrations: public policy, economics and business, and international studies.
  • The US and global application typically opens in spring and closes in early September for entry the following August.

What is Schwarzman Scholars?

Schwarzman Scholars is not a scholarship you use at a university of your choice; it is a complete, structured program. All scholars study a one-year master's in Global Affairs at Schwarzman College, Tsinghua University, in Beijing. The curriculum combines core courses with a concentration in public policy, economics and business, or international studies, plus a capstone project and a study tour across China.

The program's founding idea is that understanding China is essential for any future global leader. Scholars build a network across cultures that most graduate degrees cannot offer, which is a large part of the program's appeal.

What does the award cover?

A Schwarzman Scholars award is fully funded. It typically covers tuition and fees, room and board at Schwarzman College, travel to and from Beijing, an in-country study tour, books and supplies, a laptop, health insurance, and a monthly personal stipend for discretionary expenses.

Because nearly everything is provided, scholars can focus on the program's academic and leadership work rather than on financial planning. Verify the current funding details on the official website, schwarzmanscholars.org, before applying.

Eligibility: age, degree, and English

Eligibility for Schwarzman Scholars is clear and strict:

  • You must be at least 18 but not yet 29 years old as of August 1 of the year you would enroll.
  • You must have completed an undergraduate degree before the program begins (final-year students may apply).
  • You must demonstrate strong English ability, normally through an accepted English test unless you studied in English.

There is no fixed citizenship quota in the sense of reserved numbers; the class is deliberately international, with scholars drawn from the United States, China, and the rest of the world in roughly balanced proportion.

Selection criteria

Selection committees assess three broad qualities: leadership, intellect, and character. In practice they look for evidence that you have led initiatives with measurable results, that you think clearly and deeply about complex problems, and that you will represent the program well in the future. Your essays, recommendations, and interview are where that evidence lives.

How to apply step by step

Check your eligibility

Confirm the age rule and your degree status before investing time. If you are currently an undergraduate, confirm you will complete all requirements before enrollment.

Prepare your materials

The online application includes a resume, academic records, essays, recommendation letters, and a leadership questionnaire. Some cycles also require a short video introduction.

Write specific essays

The essays ask about your leadership experience, how you approach global challenges, and why Schwarzman Scholars is the right program for you. Specific stories and outcomes beat generic ambition.

Arrange recommendations

Choose recommenders who know you well and can speak to your leadership and character, and give them plenty of time.

Interview if shortlisted

Finalists attend interviews, often online, conducted by a selection panel. Successful candidates are notified in the months after the deadline.

Key dates and timeline

For the US and global application, Schwarzman Scholars typically opens in early spring and closes in early September (for example, September 9 in a recent cycle) for the class entering the following August. Applicants with Chinese citizenship follow a separate timeline earlier in the year. Interviews run in autumn and final decisions are announced before the end of the year. Confirm the current dates on the official website.

Tips to stand out

  • Start your essays months early; the best Schwarzman applications are rewritten several times.
  • Show leadership with outcomes: name the problem, your role, and the measurable result, following our framework for a competitive scholarship profile.
  • Tailor your essays to the program's China-focused mission rather than writing a generic study abroad essay; our statement of purpose guide shows how to make fit specific.
  • Choose recommenders who have seen you lead, and brief them on the program's values; see how to get strong letters of recommendation.
  • Keep other options open by comparing programs on our scholarship results page.

posts.title: Knight-Hennessy Scholars at Stanford: Full Guide
posts.metaDescription: Knight-Hennessy Scholars guide: Stanford's fully funded graduate fellowship for global leaders - eligibility, funding and the two applications.
posts.excerpt: A practical guide to the Knight-Hennessy Scholars program, covering funding, eligibility, the separate Stanford application, and key deadlines.

faq.q: Is the Knight-Hennessy Scholars award fully funded?
faq.a: Yes. It covers tuition and associated fees, a stipend for living and academic expenses, health insurance, and a travel allowance, for up to three years for doctoral study or the full duration of shorter programs.

faq.q: Do I need to apply to Stanford separately?
faq.a: Yes. Knight-Hennessy Scholars requires two applications: one to the fellowship and a separate application to your chosen Stanford graduate program. Both are required for consideration.

faq.q: Who can apply for Knight-Hennessy Scholars?
faq.a: Applicants of any nationality who are applying to a full-time Stanford graduate degree program. There is no age limit, and scholars come from every field.

faq.q: What is the Knight-Hennessy application deadline?
faq.a: The Knight-Hennessy application typically closes in early October. Your Stanford program application must also be submitted by its own deadline, usually by early December.

faq.q: Can I use the Knight-Hennessy award at another university?
faq.a: No. The award is tied to full-time graduate study at Stanford University and cannot be used elsewhere.

posts.bodyHtml:
The Knight-Hennessy Scholars program is Stanford University's flagship graduate fellowship, funding exceptional students from around the world to pursue any graduate degree at Stanford while taking part in a leadership-focused scholar community. The program admits up to 100 scholars each year across every field, from PhDs in engineering to law, medicine, and the MBA. The award is designed to develop leaders who can address complex global challenges with courage and creativity.

This guide explains how Knight-Hennessy Scholars works, what it covers, who can apply, and the one structural detail that confuses many applicants: it requires two separate applications, one to Knight-Hennessy and one to your Stanford degree program.

Key takeaways

  • Knight-Hennessy Scholars funds up to three years of graduate study at Stanford, covering tuition, fees, a living stipend, health insurance, and a travel allowance.
  • It is open to applicants of any nationality pursuing any full-time Stanford graduate degree, including PhD, master's, and professional programs.
  • You must submit two applications: one to Knight-Hennessy Scholars and a separate application to your Stanford graduate program.
  • The Knight-Hennessy application typically opens in June and closes in early October.
  • Selection is holistic, emphasising independence of thought, purposeful leadership, and a civic mindset.

What is Knight-Hennessy Scholars?

Knight-Hennessy Scholars is a university-wide graduate fellowship. Instead of funding a single field, it gathers scholars from all of Stanford's graduate schools into one cohort that includes weekly gatherings, workshops, and mentoring. Scholars gain the financial freedom to focus on their degree and the community to develop as leaders.

The program is named for Philip H. Knight and John Hennessy, who helped fund it, and it is deliberately multidisciplinary. The value comes partly from the award and partly from the community: PhD scientists sit alongside law students, medical researchers, and engineers.

What does the award cover?

The Knight-Hennessy Scholars award is comprehensive. It typically covers full tuition and associated fees for your Stanford degree, a stipend for living and academic expenses, health insurance, and a travel allowance to support study-related travel. For doctoral programs the award is renewable for up to three years of support; for shorter degrees it covers the full program duration.

The exact composition of the package is confirmed when you are offered the award, and you should verify current details on the official website, khn.stanford.edu.

Eligibility

Knight-Hennessy Scholars is open to applicants of every nationality, with no quotas by country or field. To be eligible you must:

  • Apply to a full-time Stanford graduate degree program for which you meet the admissions requirements.
  • Demonstrate an excellent academic record and strong leadership potential.
  • Not already hold a doctoral degree, in most cases.

There is no age limit, which makes the program unusual among prestigious fellowships. Both new applicants to any eligible Stanford program and current first-year Stanford PhD students can apply in the appropriate cycle.

Two applications, not one

The defining structural feature of Knight-Hennessy Scholars is that it requires two separate applications, and they are not optional alternatives:

  • The Knight-Hennessy Scholars application. This is the fellowship application, with essays, short answers, a resume, recommendation letters, and a video statement. It asks you to make your case for selection as a Knight-Hennessy Scholar.
  • The Stanford graduate program application. This is your standard application for admission to your chosen degree program at Stanford, with its own requirements and deadlines.

Both must be completed in the same cycle. One strong application cannot substitute for the other; if either is missing or late, you are not considered.

How to apply step by step

Choose your Stanford program

Identify the full-time graduate degree you want to pursue and confirm it is eligible. Read the program's requirements and deadline carefully.

Complete the Knight-Hennessy application

Submit the fellowship application by the Knight-Hennessy deadline, including your essays, short answers, resume, recommendations, and video statement.

Complete the Stanford application

Submit your separate Stanford graduate program application by that program's deadline for Knight-Hennessy applicants, which is typically the earlier of the program deadline or early December.

Prepare for interviews

A shortlist of finalists is interviewed in early spring. The interview focuses on your goals, your thinking, and your fit with the program's values.

Receive your decision

Decisions are announced in spring. Scholars receive both admission to their Stanford program and the Knight-Hennessy award together.

Key dates

The Knight-Hennessy application typically opens in June and closes in early October, with the exact deadline announced each year. Your Stanford program application must be submitted by that program's Knight-Hennessy deadline or by early December, whichever comes first. Interviews take place in early spring and decisions are announced in spring for entry in September. Confirm all dates on khn.stanford.edu.

Tips for a competitive application

  • Treat the two applications as one story told from two angles; our statement of purpose guide helps you make each one specific.
  • Use the essays to show independence of thought with concrete examples, following the advice in our profile guide.
  • Brief your recommenders on both programs so their letters address leadership and civic mindset; see how to get strong letters.
  • Start in summer, not September; both applications involve substantial writing.
  • Compare Knight-Hennessy with other funded US options on our scholarship results page.

posts.title: Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship: PhD Funding
posts.metaDescription: Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship guide: a $50,000 CAD per year award for doctoral study, covering eligibility, how nominations work, and deadlines.
posts.excerpt: A complete guide to the Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship, including funding, eligibility, and the nomination process for PhD study in Canada.

faq.q: What does the Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship fund?
faq.a: The award provides $50,000 CAD per year for three years of full-time doctoral study at a Canadian university. Some institutions supplement it to cover tuition and other costs.

faq.q: Can I apply directly for the Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship?
faq.a: No. You cannot apply directly. The scholarship is nomination-based: you must be nominated by a Canadian institution that has the authority to make Vanier nominations.

faq.q: Who is eligible for the Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship?
faq.a: Canadian citizens, permanent residents, and international students who have completed a first graduate degree or equivalent and are pursuing full-time doctoral study at a nominating Canadian university.

faq.q: What is the Vanier Scholarship deadline?
faq.a: The national deadline is in November, but individual universities set earlier internal deadlines for nominations. Your program's graduate office will tell you when its internal deadline falls.

faq.q: Is the Vanier Scholarship competitive?
faq.a: Yes, extremely. Institutions nominate only their strongest PhD applicants, and roughly a few hundred awards are made across Canada each year out of thousands of nominations.

posts.bodyHtml:
The Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship is the flagship doctoral award of the Canadian government, providing $50,000 CAD per year for three years to outstanding doctoral students at Canadian universities. Named after former Governor General Georges Vanier, the program rewards scholars who demonstrate academic excellence, research potential, and leadership. It is open to Canadian citizens, permanent residents, and international students alike, which makes it one of the most valuable funding routes for doctoral study in Canada.

This guide explains how the Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship works, what it covers, who is eligible, and the nomination process that every applicant must navigate. The most important fact to understand is that you do not apply directly to the government; you are nominated by a Canadian university.

Key takeaways

  • The Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship provides $50,000 CAD per year for up to three years of full-time doctoral study in Canada.
  • It is open to Canadian citizens, permanent residents, and international students at participating Canadian universities.
  • You cannot apply directly; a Canadian university must nominate you through the national process.
  • Selection is based on three equally weighted criteria: academic excellence, research potential, and leadership.
  • The national deadline is in November, but university internal deadlines come much earlier, so contact your program early.

What is the Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship?

The Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship was created to attract and support the world's top doctoral students at Canadian universities. Each year, participating universities nominate their strongest PhD applicants, and a selection board makes roughly a few hundred awards. Because the award is designed to support doctoral students across all disciplines, applicants from the humanities to the health sciences compete on the same three criteria: academic excellence, research potential, and leadership.

Winning a Vanier brings prestige as well as funding. Many universities treat Vanier nominees as priority admits, and the award is a significant line on any academic CV.

What does the award cover?

A Vanier award provides $50,000 CAD per year for three years of full-time doctoral study. That amount is fixed and does not vary by discipline or university. Because tuition and living costs can exceed this in some provinces, many host institutions add their own funding to cover tuition and fees on top of the Vanier award.

The three-year term assumes standard doctoral progress. If you need more than three years to finish, additional funding usually comes from your supervisor, department, or other sources rather than the Vanier award itself.

Eligibility

To be eligible for the Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship, you must:

  • Be a Canadian citizen, a permanent resident of Canada, or an international student.
  • Have completed a first graduate degree or equivalent, such as a master's degree, before taking up the award.
  • Pursue full-time doctoral study at a Canadian university with Vanier nomination authority.
  • Not hold or have previously held a Vanier award.

In special cases, outstanding students who do not yet hold a master's degree but meet very high standards may be considered, but these cases are rare. Direct-entry PhD students are eligible if they meet the degree requirement by the start of the award.

How the nomination process works

The Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship is nomination-based. The process has three stages:

1. Connect with a Canadian supervisor

Before anything else, you need admission (or near-certain admission) to a PhD program at a Canadian university and a supervisor who supports your nomination. Your supervisor and department are the ones who put you forward.

2. University internal selection

Each university has a quota of Vanier nominations. Departments propose candidates, and the university's internal committee selects its strongest candidates. Internal deadlines are usually weeks before the national deadline, so contact the graduate office as early as possible.

3. National competition

Nominated candidates submit their complete application through the national system by the November deadline. The tri-agency selection board reviews all nominations and announces awards in the spring.

Because institutions can nominate only a limited number of candidates, being nominated means your university already considers you one of its very best doctoral applicants.

Key documents in the application

The Vanier application consists of several parts, all prepared with your university:

  • A research proposal outlining your doctoral project, its importance, and your qualifications to carry it out.
  • Leadership contributions, where you describe activities that demonstrate leadership, from mentoring to community engagement.
  • Recommendation letters, including one from a referee who can attest to your academic and research abilities and one for leadership, in most cases.
  • Your CV and transcripts.

Getting these documents right is where most candidates make or break their application. Your supervisor and graduate office will have templates and examples, and you should give them several drafts.

Key dates

The national deadline for the Vanier Canada Graduate Scholarship is typically in early to mid-November each year, with awards announced the following spring. However, each university sets an earlier internal deadline for nomination submissions, and popular programs may require you to signal interest months before that. Contact your prospective university's graduate studies office at least a year before you intend to start your PhD to confirm its internal timeline.

Tips for a strong application

  • Start supervisor conversations early, because a supportive supervisor is the single biggest factor in a successful nomination.
  • Make the research proposal precise: clear question, method, and significance, written so an expert can see you are ready to execute it.
  • Document leadership with evidence and outcomes, applying the approach in our profile guide.
  • Choose referees who can speak separately to your research and your leadership, and brief them following our recommendation guide.
  • Ask your program's graduate office for past successful applications; their feedback will sharpen yours.
  • Compare Vanier with other funded PhD routes on our scholarship results page.

posts.title: Marshall Scholarship: Study in the UK for US Students
posts.metaDescription: Marshall Scholarship guide: fully funded postgraduate study in the UK for US citizens, covering eligibility, funding, deadlines, and how to apply.
posts.excerpt: A complete guide to the Marshall Scholarship for US students, covering what it funds, eligibility, the selection timeline, and application strategy.

faq.q: Is the Marshall Scholarship fully funded?
faq.a: Yes. It covers university fees, a cost-of-living allowance, an annual book and travel allowance, airfare, and a grant for dependent children in some cases. It is a full-cost award.

faq.q: Who is eligible for the Marshall Scholarship?
faq.a: US citizens who hold a bachelor's degree with a strong GPA (typically a minimum 3.7 or 3.8) and who will not have completed a US postgraduate degree before the scholarship begins. You must be under a maximum age, usually 29 at the time of application.

faq.q: What is the Marshall Scholarship deadline?
faq.a: The application typically opens in early spring and closes in late September for awards the following year. Regional interviews are held in the autumn.

faq.q: How many Marshall Scholarships are awarded?
faq.a: Up to around 40 awards are made each year across the US, selected through the regional application process.

faq.q: Can I use a Marshall Scholarship at any UK university?
faq.a: Yes. Scholars choose any accredited UK university and any field of study, from the sciences to the humanities, as long as it is a postgraduate program.

posts.bodyHtml:
The Marshall Scholarship is one of the most prestigious American postgraduate awards, funding outstanding US citizens to study any subject at any UK university. Established in 1953 in gratitude for the Marshall Plan, the program aims to strengthen the special relationship between the United States and the United Kingdom by sending promising American leaders to study in Britain. Each year, up to around 40 scholars are selected through a competitive regional process.

This guide explains how the Marshall Scholarship works, what it covers, who can apply, and how to move through the selection timeline, including the regional interview that most finalists face.

Key takeaways

  • The Marshall Scholarship funds full-cost postgraduate study at any UK university for outstanding US citizens.
  • It covers university fees, a living allowance, a book and travel allowance, airfare, and more.
  • Applicants must be US citizens, hold a strong bachelor's degree, and typically be under 29 at the time of application.
  • The application opens in early spring and closes in late September, with regional interviews in the autumn.
  • Selection emphasises academic excellence, leadership, ambassadorial potential, and a serious plan for study in the UK.

What is the Marshall Scholarship?

The Marshall Scholarship was founded as a living memorial to the Marshall Plan and the ideals of the Anglo-American alliance. It is open to US citizens in any field, at any accredited UK university, for one to three years of postgraduate study. Scholars join a network of leaders in government, academia, the arts, business, and journalism, and the program actively cultivates ties between scholars and their British counterparts.

Because the scholarship allows nearly complete freedom in choice of university and subject, it attracts a very broad applicant pool, from STEM researchers to historians and policy students.

What does the award cover?

A Marshall Scholarship is a full-cost award. It typically covers the cost of university fees, a living allowance to cover accommodation and everyday expenses, an annual allowance for books and personal travel, airfare between the United States and the United Kingdom, and a travel grant for dependent children in certain circumstances. Marshall scholars who need an extra year to complete a one-year course may sometimes receive additional support for a second year.

Exact amounts are set annually, so confirm the current package on the official website, marshallscholarship.org, when you apply.

Eligibility

To be eligible for a Marshall Scholarship, you must:

  • Be a citizen of the United States of America.
  • Hold a bachelor's degree from an accredited US institution with a strong record, typically a GPA of 3.7 or above.
  • Not have completed a postgraduate degree, and not be enrolled in one that would complete before the award starts.
  • Be under a maximum age, usually 29, at the time of application.

There is no restriction on field of study. Most Marshall scholars are in their final undergraduate year or recently graduated, and a large share have significant leadership or research experience already.

How the selection process works

Applications are submitted through regional committees covering different parts of the United States. The process runs in stages:

Written application

You submit personal and academic information, a study proposal, essays, and recommendation letters through the online system.

Regional selection

Each region reviews its applicants and selects a shortlist of candidates.

Regional interview

Shortlisted candidates attend a panel interview in their region. The panel tests your academic plans, your leadership and character, and your ability to represent the scholarship's aims.

National selection

Regional committees forward their recommendations, and the national selection committee makes the final decisions. Scholars are announced in early winter.

Key dates

The Marshall Scholarship application typically opens in early spring and closes in late September for awards the following academic year. Regional interviews are held in October and November, and final decisions are announced in December. Because your UK university offers must align with the scholarship timeline, you may also need to apply to universities in parallel. Check marshallscholarship.org for the exact dates in your cycle.

Key documents in the application

  • Study proposal. A detailed plan for your postgraduate study in the UK, including your choice of university and course and why the UK is the right place for it.
  • Personal statement. Your story, your leadership, and your vision, written for the scholarship's values.
  • Recommendations. Letters from professors and others who know your academic work and character.
  • Transcripts and CV. Evidence of your academic record and experience.

Tips for a competitive application

  • Build your candidacy over years, not weeks: research, leadership roles, and public service all matter; see our profile guide.
  • Make your study proposal concrete and justified by the UK context, using the essay techniques in our statement of purpose guide.
  • Request letters early and brief your referees on the scholarship's criteria, following our recommendation guide.
