  • Practice interviews with friends and mentors; regional panels value poise and genuine answers over rehearsed lines.
  • Explore other funded UK options as a backup on our scholarship results page.

posts.title: KAIST International Scholarships Guide
posts.metaDescription: KAIST International Scholarships: full tuition waivers, monthly stipends and health insurance for students at Korea's top science university.
posts.excerpt: A practical guide to KAIST scholarships for international students, covering the KAIST International Scholarship, funding levels, and the application process.

faq.q: Is the KAIST International Scholarship fully funded?
faq.a: It is a full-tuition award and more: it covers the full cost of tuition, provides a monthly stipend for living expenses, and offers national health insurance for international students.

faq.q: Who is eligible for KAIST scholarships?
faq.a: Newly admitted international students applying for KAIST degree programs, including bachelor's, master's, and doctoral programs, who are not already benefiting from other government or KAIST scholarships.

faq.q: How much is the KAIST monthly stipend?
faq.a: The monthly stipend for graduate students is around KRW 350,000 per month, plus the full tuition waiver. Exact figures are set each year and confirmed in your admission offer.

faq.q: Do I need to apply for a KAIST scholarship separately?
faq.a: No. International applicants to KAIST degree programs are automatically considered for the KAIST International Scholarship through their admission application. It is not a separate form.

faq.q: What are the KAIST application deadlines?
faq.a: KAIST runs multiple admissions tracks with deadlines that vary by program, typically in the autumn and spring. Check the official admission site for the track and deadline that applies to you.

posts.bodyHtml:
The KAIST International Scholarships are the main funding route for international students at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, South Korea's leading research university in science and technology. KAIST offers full-tuition scholarships, monthly stipends, and health insurance to international students across its undergraduate and graduate programs. Because the scholarships are awarded automatically through the admission application, many students do not realise how accessible the funding is.

This guide explains how KAIST International Scholarships work, what they cover, who is eligible, and how the application process fits together. If you want a fully funded education in engineering, science, or technology in Asia, KAIST is one of the strongest options.

Key takeaways

  • The KAIST International Scholarship covers full tuition for international students plus a monthly living stipend.
  • It also provides national health insurance to international students during their studies.
  • The scholarship is automatic: you are considered when you apply for admission to a KAIST degree program, with no separate form.
  • Graduate students in many programs can combine the scholarship with research assistantship pay from their lab.
  • Deadlines vary by admissions track, so plan around your program's specific application window.

What is the KAIST International Scholarship?

KAIST, based in Daejeon, South Korea, is a research university founded in 1971 to train scientists and engineers. It is consistently ranked among the best universities in Asia and the world for engineering and technology. To attract top international talent, KAIST funds incoming international students through the KAIST International Scholarship, which is granted automatically based on admission merit.

This design is unusual and valuable: instead of requiring a separate scholarship essay and timeline, the scholarship rides on your admission application. If you are admitted as an international student, you typically receive the funding as part of your offer.

What does the scholarship cover?

The KAIST International Scholarship is a comprehensive package. It typically covers:

  • Full tuition. The entire cost of tuition for your degree program is waived.
  • A monthly stipend. You receive a monthly allowance for living expenses; for graduate students this is around KRW 350,000 per month, and for undergraduates it varies by level.
  • Health insurance. KAIST supports international students with national health insurance coverage.

Graduate students who join research labs also earn research assistantship salaries from their professors, which can add significantly to the base stipend. Confirm the exact current figures on the official admission website, admission.kaist.ac.kr, before you apply.

Eligibility

You are eligible for a KAIST International Scholarship if you are an international applicant applying to a KAIST degree program, whether bachelor's, master's, or doctoral. You must not be receiving another scholarship that already covers your tuition and fees. Students on government scholarships such as the Global Korea Scholarship may not be able to combine the two, so check the terms of each funding source.

There is no separate scholarship application. Admission to KAIST as an international student is what triggers the award, though the exact level of funding can depend on the program and admissions track.

How to apply step by step

Choose your program and track

KAIST runs its admissions through the Graduate Admissions or Undergraduate Admissions system, with multiple tracks per year. Confirm which track is open for your program and read its requirements.

Prepare your application documents

You will need transcripts, degree certificates, a statement of purpose, recommendation letters, proof of English proficiency, and your passport details. Requirements vary by program.

Submit the online application

Complete the online application by your track's deadline. The scholarship consideration is included automatically, so there is no additional scholarship step.

Await the admission decision

Admission results are announced several weeks after the deadline. If you are admitted, your offer letter will state the scholarship you have been awarded, including the stipend level.

Secure your visa and arrive

Accepted students arrange a D-2 student visa through the Korean embassy or consulate and complete any required documents before arrival.

Key dates

KAIST International Scholarships follow the admission calendar, not a separate scholarship calendar. Graduate admission tracks typically open in the autumn and close in early winter or spring depending on the program, with a second track in some years. Undergraduate admission runs similar cycles. Check admission.kaist.ac.kr for the deadlines that apply to your program and track, and begin document preparation weeks ahead.

Tips for a strong application

  • Line up recommendation letters from professors who know your research or academic potential, using our recommendation guide.
  • Write a focused statement of purpose that shows fit with your chosen lab or program, following our SOP guide.
  • Prepare your English test early, since KAIST requires proof of proficiency.
  • Start by building the research and academic record that admissions committees reward, as covered in our profile guide.
  • Compare KAIST with other Asian options like the Global Korea Scholarship on our scholarship results page.

posts.title: Academic Conferences That Fund Student Travel
posts.metaDescription: Academic conferences that fund student attendance: fee waivers, travel grants, and registration discounts from IEEE, ACM, and university-backed events.
posts.excerpt: A list of academic conferences and funding mechanisms that help students attend, including travel grants, fee waivers, and volunteering discounts.

faq.q: Can students really get conferences to pay for attendance?
faq.a: Yes. Major conference organisers, professional societies such as IEEE and ACM, and many universities offer travel grants, fee waivers, and registration discounts specifically for students, especially those presenting papers or posters.

faq.q: Do I need to present a paper to get conference funding?
faq.a: Not always. Many student travel grants require a paper, poster, or presentation, but some cover general attendees, and volunteer programs trade registration fees for help with the event.

faq.q: What do conference travel grants typically cover?
faq.a: Awards vary widely: some cover the full registration fee, others reimburse flights and hotel costs, and many provide a fixed dollar amount (for example, a few hundred to over a thousand dollars) toward total costs.

faq.q: Where do I find conference travel grants?
faq.a: Start with the conference's own website, then check professional societies, your department and graduate school, your supervisor's research grants, and national funding bodies in your field.

faq.q: When should I apply for conference funding?
faq.a: As soon as you know your paper was accepted. Most grants open months before the event and close four to eight weeks before it, so apply early and keep the acceptance letter handy.

posts.bodyHtml:
Academic conferences are where research gets seen, networks get built, and opportunities get created, but the cost of registration, flights, and hotels keeps many students away. The good news is that a surprising number of conferences fund student attendance directly. Between student travel grants, fee waivers, registration discounts, and volunteer programs, most students can attend at least one major conference a year without paying full price.

This guide covers the best-known conferences and programmes that fund student attendance, and, just as importantly, the funding mechanisms that exist inside almost every conference. The strategy is simple: find a conference that accepts your work, get your paper or poster accepted, and apply for the student support that most organisers provide.

Key takeaways

  • IEEE and ACM both run student travel grant programmes that support conference attendance across dozens of technical fields.
  • Many major conferences, including NeurIPS, ICML, ACL, CHI, and SIGGRAPH, offer dedicated student travel grants and volunteer registration discounts.
  • Field-specific meetings such as AGU, ASCB, and large medical conferences fund student travel through society grants and competitive awards.
  • University sources, supervisor grants, and national funding bodies fill the gaps when a conference itself has no student fund.
  • Apply as early as possible: grants are usually announced months ahead and close before the conference begins.

Conferences with strong student travel funding

Computer science and AI

The AI and machine learning community is the most generous when it comes to funding students. NeurIPS and ICML run major travel award programmes that cover registration, flights, and accommodation for selected students, with special programmes for underrepresented groups. ACL (computational linguistics) offers the same model, and CHI (human-computer interaction) and SIGGRAPH (computer graphics) fund student volunteers and travel. The IEEE and ACM student travel grant programmes are broader, supporting any accepted paper at an affiliated conference.

Engineering and applied sciences

IEEE conferences across power, electronics, communications, and robotics routinely offer student travel grants, often funded by IEEE societies such as the Computer Society and the Communications Society. ACM similarly funds students attending its flagship conferences. In many cases you need only an accepted paper and a faculty recommendation to qualify.

Natural sciences and medicine

The American Geophysical Union (AGU) supports student and early-career travel to its fall meeting. The American Society for Cell Biology (ASCB) funds student travel with competitive awards. Large medical and public health conferences frequently offer trainee travel awards and registration fee waivers for first authors, so check the funding page of any conference in your discipline before assuming you cannot afford it.

How student funding at conferences actually works

When a conference lists a travel grant, the mechanism is usually one of four types:

  • Registration fee waiver. Your registration is reduced or eliminated, which saves the biggest single expense.
  • Fixed travel award. You receive a set amount, often a few hundred to over a thousand dollars, toward flights, hotels, and food.
  • Reimbursement. You pay costs up front and claim them back after the conference with receipts.
  • Volunteer programme. You work a few hours at the event and your registration fee is waived or heavily discounted.

Most competitive grants require an accepted paper or poster and expect you to present it, so acceptance comes first and funding second.

Where to find the funding

1. The conference itself

Almost every major conference has a travel grant or student support page. Search the conference site for words like "travel grant", "student travel", "fee waiver", and "diversity support".

2. Professional societies

IEEE and ACM run the two largest student travel grant systems in the technical world. National academies and field societies (such as the Royal Society or your national physics, chemistry, or medical societies) also fund student conference travel.

3. Your university

Graduate schools, departments, and faculty research grants are a major source of conference funding. Most PhD supervisors have travel money in their grants and simply need to be asked with a clear budget.

4. National bodies and foundations

Some national research agencies and non-profit foundations fund student conference attendance in specific fields. These tend to be competitive and aligned with research priorities.

How to apply for a conference travel grant

  • Get accepted first. Apply to the conference, and use the acceptance letter in your grant application.
  • Start early. Travel grant deadlines are often two to three months before the conference.
  • Prepare a one-page case. State your accepted paper or poster, your costs, and how attending benefits your research; combine this with the advice in our profile guide.
  • Ask your supervisor. Faculty grants are the most flexible funding of all; a short request with a realistic budget often succeeds.
  • Apply to several sources. You can combine a fee waiver with a university grant, and if two sources over-fund you, ask one to redirect the balance.

Conference papers lead to more funding

Presenting at a conference is itself a strong item on a scholarship application. Reviewers look for students who already operate at research level, so a conference presentation strengthens your case for major awards like the ones on our scholarship results page. If you are new to research, start with the poster track or a regional conference, then work up to flagship events, and let each presentation fund the next.

posts.title: How to Get Funding for Academic Conferences
posts.focusKeyword: scholarship to attend an academic conference
posts.metaDescription: How to get a scholarship to attend an academic conference: travel grants, fee waivers, society funding, and university support explained step by step.
posts.excerpt: A step-by-step guide to funding your conference trip through travel grants, fee waivers, society awards, and university support.

faq.q: What is a conference scholarship?
faq.a: A conference scholarship is any award that pays for part or all of your conference attendance. It can be a fee waiver, a fixed travel grant, a reimbursement, or a volunteer arrangement that trades work for free registration.

faq.q: Do I need to present a paper to get a conference scholarship?
faq.a: Most competitive travel grants require an accepted paper, poster, or presentation, but volunteer programmes and some diversity and inclusion funds support attendees without an accepted paper.

faq.q: How much funding can I get for a conference?
faq.a: It varies widely. Fee waivers remove the registration cost, fixed grants range from a few hundred to well over a thousand dollars, and university funding can cover full travel and accommodation when a supervisor's grant allows it.

faq.q: What should a conference travel grant application include?
faq.a: A clear statement of what you will present, a realistic budget, a justification of why attending matters for your research and career, your CV, and any supporting letter your department can provide.

faq.q: How early should I apply for conference funding?
faq.a: As soon as your paper is accepted and often before. Travel grant deadlines fall two to three months ahead of the conference, so work backwards from the event date.

posts.bodyHtml:
Conferences are expensive, but a scholarship to attend an academic conference is more achievable than most students think. Conference organisers, professional societies, universities, and individual supervisors all fund student travel. The key is knowing which funding fits your situation and applying in the right order. Most students who attend major conferences do not pay for them themselves.

This guide walks through the five routes to conference funding, what each application requires, and the exact sequence that wins the most support. You can combine routes, so think of conference funding as a stack of sources rather than a single lottery.

Key takeaways

  • Accepted papers and posters are the key that unlocks most conference funding.
  • Professional societies such as IEEE and ACM run student travel grant programmes that fund dozens of conferences.
  • Your supervisor's research grant is often the fastest and most flexible source of conference money.
  • Volunteer programmes and diversity and inclusion funds support students without accepted papers.
  • Apply months early, stack several sources, and keep every receipt for reimbursement claims.

Route 1: Conference-organised travel grants

The first place to look is the conference itself. Major conferences in computer science, engineering, the sciences, and medicine run student travel grant programmes, sometimes funded by the conference budget and sometimes by affiliated societies. These grants typically require an accepted paper or poster and cover part or all of the costs of attending.

Read the conference's travel support page carefully, because programmes differ: some are competitive with their own application and deadline, while others award a fixed amount automatically to every accepted student presenter. Apply at the same time you submit your paper, not after it is accepted, if the grant deadline comes earlier.

Route 2: Professional society awards

Professional societies fund student attendance on a scale that surprises many students. The IEEE and ACM travel grant systems support student attendance at their affiliated conferences across dozens of fields, and field-specific societies in physics, chemistry, biology, medicine, and the humanities run their own awards. Society travel grants are usually open to society members, so joining your field's society early, often with a student discount, is a smart investment.

Look also for special programmes: many societies fund students from underrepresented groups, from developing countries, or working on specific topics. These targeted funds are often less competitive because fewer people know about them.

Route 3: University and departmental funding

Many students never ask their own university for conference money, which is a mistake. Graduate schools, departments, and faculties routinely fund student conference travel, and the application is often a single form plus a supervisor's signature. The money can be a fixed annual amount per student or drawn from a research training budget, and it frequently covers registration, flights, and accommodation.

The fastest route of all is your supervisor's research grant. Most supervisors hold grant money for travel and are happy to fund a student presenting work from the lab. Prepare a short email with your accepted abstract, the conference dates, and an itemised budget, and you will usually get a yes.

Route 4: Fee waivers and volunteer programmes

If your conference has no travel grant, reduce the cost at the source. Many conferences offer registration fee waivers or discounts for students who present, volunteer, or register early. Volunteer programmes in particular trade a few hours of event work for free or heavily discounted registration, which can save several hundred dollars at large conferences.

Some conferences also fund attendees without an accepted paper through diversity and inclusion programmes designed to widen participation. If you cannot present yet, attending on a volunteer or inclusion grant still builds the network and skills you need for your first accepted paper.

Route 5: National bodies and foundations

National research agencies, academies, and charitable foundations fund conference attendance, especially for research aligned with their priorities. These awards are competitive and usually require a recommendation or a supporting statement, but they can cover the full cost of an international trip. Search for "[your field] travel grant" and check the funding pages of national research bodies in your country.

How to apply: the winning sequence

1. Start with the conference deadline

Work backwards from the conference date. Note the paper deadline, the travel grant deadline, and the university funding deadline on a calendar, because they are usually different.

2. Get your paper accepted

Submit your abstract or paper early. An acceptance letter is the strongest single document in any conference funding application.

3. Apply to the conference grant first

Apply to the conference's own travel grant, then add society awards and university funding on top. Many students receive a conference grant and a university grant that together cover everything.

4. Ask your supervisor directly

Send a short, professional request with your acceptance letter and a budget. Grant-funded supervisors can usually say yes immediately.

5. Keep every receipt

Grants that reimburse costs require receipts, so save all booking confirmations and invoices. Ask each funder for a written confirmation of what is covered.

Building conference funding into your scholarship strategy

Conference presentations are not just line items on a CV; they are evidence of research-level ability that major scholarship committees look for. A strong profile combines awards, research, and leadership, and conference travel sits at the intersection of all three. If you are building your case for a major scholarship, present at conferences first and use the experience to strengthen every later application, whether that is a department travel fund or the flagship awards listed on our scholarship results page.

Treat conference funding like any scholarship application, and it becomes a reliable pipeline rather than a lucky break. Start with a small regional conference, then use the pattern again for a flagship international event. Each award funds the next step.

posts.title: IELTS Score Required for a Visa: by Country 2026
posts.focusKeyword: IELTS score required for a visa
posts.metaDescription: The exact IELTS band score required for student, work and PR visas in 2026, country by country, plus which IELTS test type you need.
posts.excerpt: The 2026 IELTS visa score table: minimum bands for student, work and PR routes across the UK, Canada, Australia, NZ and 10 more countries.
posts.bodyHtml:
Your English test can make or break a visa application, so the exact IELTS score required for a visa is one of the first things you should research, not the last. The score you need depends entirely on the country, the visa type and the institution, and the differences are bigger than most applicants expect: the UK will accept band 4.0 for a skilled worker visa while the same country's universities want 6.5 or higher. This guide sets out the 2026 requirements for student, work and permanent-residence visas across 14 countries, plus which IELTS test type you actually need.

Every requirement below is a minimum for the visa route. University courses almost always set their own higher bar, so always check the specific program before you book a test date.

Key takeaways

  • Choose the right test: IELTS Academic for study, IELTS General Training for most work/PR routes, IELTS for UKVI for UK visas, and IELTS Life Skills for UK family routes.
  • Canada: IELTS 6.0 overall (no band below 5.5) for the former SDS, and CLB 7–9 (IELTS 6.0+ per band) for Express Entry points.
  • UK: 5.5 in each band (B2) for the Student route; 4.0 in each band (B1) for Skilled Worker; 4.0 (Life Skills B1) for settlement.
  • Australia: 6.0 overall (5.0 minimum per band) for a student visa; 6.5+ for skilled migration points.
  • New Zealand: 5.5–6.5 for study depending on level; 6.5 overall for Skilled Migrant.
  • Your IELTS result is valid for two years, and computer-delivered results arrive in three to five days.

Which IELTS test type do you need?

Choosing the wrong test is one of the most common, and most expensive, mistakes applicants make.

  • IELTS Academic — university study, scholarships, professional registration.
  • IELTS General Training — work visas, immigration and PR (Canada Express Entry, Australia skilled visas, NZ Skilled Migrant, UK Skilled Worker).
  • IELTS for UKVI (Academic or General) — UK visa applications, taken at a UKVI-approved centre as a SELT.
  • IELTS Life Skills (A1, A2, B1) — UK family and settlement visas, speaking and listening only.

For Canadian immigration always use IELTS General Training. For UK visas use IELTS for UKVI. For university admissions, IELTS Academic is almost always required.

Required IELTS scores by country & visa (2026)

Canada

Student: 6.0 overall with no band below 5.5 was the SDS benchmark; most universities ask 6.0–6.5. PR: Express Entry maps IELTS to CLB levels, with CLB 7 (IELTS 6.0 per band) as the minimum and CLB 9 for maximum points. IELTS General Training is the right version.

United States

The F-1 student visa has no federal IELTS minimum; each university sets its own bar, typically 6.0–7.5. Work (H-1B) and green card routes do not require IELTS.

United Kingdom

Student route: 5.5 in each band (B2). Skilled Worker: 4.0 in each band (B1). Settlement/ILR: 4.0 via IELTS Life Skills B1. The Graduate visa needs no test.

Australia

Student visa (500): 6.0 overall with a 5.0 minimum per band. Graduate visa (485): 6.5 overall. Skilled visas: 6.0 per band earns points, and higher bands earn more.

New Zealand

Study: 5.5–6.5 depending on qualification level. Skilled Migrant Category: 6.5 overall is the typical bar, and higher scores improve your profile.

Germany, Netherlands, France, Italy, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Turkey

None of these countries requires IELTS for the visa itself, but English-taught programs at their universities set their own minimums: typically 6.0–6.5 for most of Europe, 6.5–7.0 for top Swiss schools like ETH Zurich and EPFL, and 5.5–6.5 for Turkish universities. "Not required" for a visa means the English bar is met through other evidence, never that no English is needed.

IELTS test fees and validity (2026)

Fees are set locally and differ between computer-delivered and paper tests. Typical 2026 ranges: India INR 17,000–18,500; Pakistan PKR 53,000–62,000; UK £215–235; US$235–270; Canada CAD 319–340; Australia AUD 485–525. Results: computer-delivered in three to five days, paper in 13 days. Your Test Report Form is valid for two years for visas and university applications, and with One Skill Retake you can resit a single module within 60 days.

How to prepare

A structured plan beats random practice every time. Focus on your weakest module first, take timed practice tests weekly, and build daily listening exposure. Our IELTS 7+ in 6 weeks plan gives a week-by-week structure, and the TOEFL vs IELTS comparison helps you pick the right test if you have a choice. For the full requirements table, test-centre locator and booking steps, see our IELTS guidance hub, and for country-by-country visa details use the visa guidance page.

faq.q: What IELTS score do I need for a student visa in 2026?
faq.a: Most universities and student visa routes require IELTS 6.0 to 6.5 overall. The UK Student route accepts 5.5 in each band (B2), Australia requires 6.0 overall with a 5.0 minimum per band, and Canada's benchmark was 6.0 overall with no band below 5.5.

faq.q: Is IELTS required for permanent residence?
faq.a: In points-based systems, yes: Canada's Express Entry, Australia's skilled migration and New Zealand's Skilled Migrant Category all award points for IELTS bands (Canada maps IELTS to CLB, with CLB 9 giving maximum points). Most European PR routes do not ask for IELTS.

faq.q: What is the difference between IELTS Academic and General Training?
faq.a: Academic is for university study and professional registration; General Training is for work, immigration and PR. Listening and Speaking are identical; Reading and Writing differ, with Academic using academic texts and data-description tasks and General Training using everyday texts and a letter-writing task.

faq.q: How long is an IELTS score valid?
faq.a: Two years from the test date for universities and visa authorities. Visa applications almost always require a result issued within the last two years.

faq.q: How much does IELTS cost in 2026?
faq.a: Typical ranges: India INR 17,000–18,500, Pakistan PKR 53,000–62,000, UK £215–235, USA US$235–270, Canada CAD 319–340, Australia AUD 485–525. Computer tests sometimes cost a little more; One Skill Retake is around 70–80% of the full fee.

posts.title: DV Lottery 2027: How to Enter the US Green Card Lottery
posts.metaDescription: DV Lottery 2027 guide: eligibility, the new passport and $1 fee rules, how to enter, costs, results and how to avoid scams.
posts.excerpt: How to enter the DV-2027 Diversity Visa lottery, including the new passport requirement, the $1 entry fee, eligibility and scam warnings.
posts.bodyHtml:
The DV Lottery 2027 is the US Diversity Visa program for fiscal year 2027, the annual draw that gives up to 55,000 permanent resident visas (green cards) to people from countries with historically low immigration to the United States. It is completely random: about 10 million people enter each cycle and roughly 55,000 are selected, which makes it a genuine lottery and the only US immigration route most applicants can try without an employer, a family sponsor or an investment. This guide covers the DV-2027 eligibility rules, the new passport and $1 fee requirements, how to enter, and how to avoid the scams that surround the program.

DV-2027 covers the US fiscal year running from October 1, 2026 to September 30, 2027. As of this guide's publication the registration window had not yet opened — the State Department delayed it while introducing new entry rules — so the most important advice is to monitor the official portal and prepare your documents now.

Key takeaways

  • DV-2027 awards up to 55,000 green cards; entry is free to file aside from a new $1 fee, and registration happens only at dvprogram.state.gov.
  • New for DV-2027 (effective April 10, 2026): you need a valid, unexpired passport at entry and must upload a scan of the biographic and signature pages.
  • Eligibility depends on your country of birth, plus either a high-school education or two years of qualifying work experience in the last five years.
  • You may submit only one entry; multiple entries disqualify you.
  • Results appear only on the Entrant Status Check page; the State Department never emails, mails or phones winners.
  • If selected, the visa must be issued before September 30, 2027, with no extensions.

What is the DV Lottery?

Created by the Immigration Act of 1990, the Diversity Visa program broadens the mix of nationalities among US immigrants by giving visas to people from countries that sent few immigrants in the previous five years. "High-admission" countries whose natives cannot enter include India, China (mainland), Mexico, Nigeria, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Brazil, Canada, the Philippines, South Korea, Vietnam and the UK (mainland-born), among others, and the list shifts each cycle, so always check the official instructions.

Eligibility for DV-2027

You qualify if you were born in an eligible country and meet one of two standards: a high-school education or its equivalent (a 12-year course of schooling), or, within the five years before applying, two years of work experience in an occupation requiring at least two years of training or experience. Two family rules expand the pool: if your spouse or parent was born in an eligible country, you may derive eligibility, and under cross-chargeability a married couple can often use the eligible spouse's birth country.

The new DV-2027 entry rules

A final rule effective April 10, 2026 changed how entries work. First, every entrant must have a valid, unexpired passport at the time of entry and upload a JPEG scan of the biographic and signature pages (maximum 5 MB). Limited exemptions exist for stateless persons and nationals of Communist-controlled countries unable to obtain a passport. Second, every entry requires a non-refundable $1 fee, paid through Pay.gov, with no waivers. The form now asks for your date of birth and sex rather than age and gender. The State Department delayed the registration window to give applicants time to obtain passports.

How to enter, step by step

  1. Get a valid passport now and scan the biographic and signature pages as a JPEG under 5 MB.
  2. Wait for the official registration window to open, announced on travel.state.gov and dvprogram.state.gov — do not enter through any third-party site.
  3. Complete the entry form (DS-5501) in one sitting; there is no save-and-return option, so budget about 90 minutes.
  4. Submit exactly one entry per person and keep your confirmation page and unique confirmation number.
  5. After the window closes, check results only on the Entrant Status Check page using your confirmation number, last name and date of birth.

If you are selected

Selection is not a visa; it is an invitation to apply. You must complete the DS-260 immigrant visa application, attend a consular interview and pay a non-refundable diversity visa fee of $330 per person (principal and each family member), plus a separate USCIS immigrant fee before your green card is mailed. Higher case numbers may only become current in the Visa Bulletin near the end of the fiscal year, so a complete file early is your best protection. Every step must finish before September 30, 2027 or the opportunity expires.

Avoiding DV-2027 scams

Scammers thrive on this program. No one can increase your selection odds, and winners are never notified by email, post or phone. Any site charging you to "guarantee" entry, or an agent offering to submit for a fee, is a scam, since the State Department says entrants should complete the form themselves. The only official addresses are dvprogram.state.gov (entry and status) and travel.state.gov (instructions and news). For the wider picture on US immigration and study, see our immigrate to the USA guide and the study in the USA guide.

faq.q: When does DV-2027 registration open?
faq.a: The State Department delayed the DV-2027 entry window to give applicants time to obtain passports and announced that exact dates would follow on travel.state.gov and dvprogram.state.gov. As of August 2026 the window had not yet opened, so monitor those official pages rather than any third-party source.

faq.q: Who can enter the DV Lottery 2027?
faq.a: You must have been born in an eligible (low-admission) country and have either a high-school education or two years of qualifying work experience in the last five years. You can also derive eligibility from your spouse or parents' birth country, and cross-chargeability may apply for married couples.

faq.q: How much does it cost to enter the DV Lottery?
faq.a: Registration itself is $1 (the new non-refundable entry fee paid via Pay.gov), with no waivers. If selected, you pay a $330 diversity visa processing fee per person at the consular interview plus a separate USCIS immigrant fee before the green card is mailed.

faq.q: What are the new DV-2027 passport and photo rules?
faq.a: You need a valid, unexpired passport at entry and must upload a JPEG scan of its biographic and signature pages (max 5 MB). Limited exemptions apply for stateless persons and nationals of Communist-controlled countries who cannot obtain a passport.

faq.q: How do I know if I won the DV lottery?
faq.a: Only through the Entrant Status Check page at dvprogram.state.gov, using your confirmation number, last name and date of birth. The State Department never emails, mails or phones winners, and anyone claiming to do so is running a scam.

posts.title: How to Immigrate to Switzerland: 2026 Permits, Quotas & PR
posts.metaDescription: How to immigrate to Switzerland in 2026: the 8,500-permit quota, B and L permits, the labour-market test, and the 10-year path to PR.
posts.excerpt: The honest 2026 guide to immigrating to Switzerland: quotas, the precedence rule, B and L permits, salaries and how long PR really takes.
posts.bodyHtml:
Switzerland is the hardest country in Europe to immigrate to, and the most honest about why. For third-country nationals (everyone outside the EU/EFTA) there is no points system and no fixed salary threshold: admission is quota-based, with 8,500 permits for 2026, and governed by a strict labour-market-precedence rule that puts Swiss and EU/EFTA candidates first. If you are exceptional in a field of economic interest, a Switzerland work permit can happen; for junior and mid-level applicants, it is a lottery ticket rather than a plan A. This guide explains exactly how the system works and the realistic paths in.

The good news is that the rules are clear, the quotas do sometimes go unused (utilisation ran around 74% of L and B permits in 2024), and the study route offers a genuine, if not guaranteed, foot in the door. Here is how to plan it.

Key takeaways

  • No EU Blue Card and no points system in Switzerland: third-country admission runs on employer-driven quotas (8,500 permits in 2026).
  • You need a job offer from a Swiss employer, who must prove no Swiss or EU/EFTA candidate was available (the precedence rule).
  • The B residence permit and L short-stay permit both require a university degree or equivalent plus relevant experience in an occupation of economic interest.
  • There is no salary threshold, but pay must match local market terms; processing runs 2–6 months via the canton then SEM.
  • Permanent residence (C permit) comes after 10 years for most third-country nationals; citizenship takes 10 years plus integration.
  • There is no digital-nomad visa, no golden visa, and a tourist visa cannot be converted into a work permit.

How Swiss work permits work

Switzerland reserves its labour market for Swiss and EU/EFTA nationals first. Third-country nationals qualify only as "managers, specialists and qualified persons" in occupations of economic interest, with a university degree or equivalent experience, and only when no Swiss or EU candidate is available. Employers apply for your permit through the canton, which forwards to the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM). The 2026 quota is 8,500 permits: 4,500 B residence permits and 4,000 L short-stay permits, with separate quotas for EU/EFTA service providers (3,500) and UK nationals (3,500).

B vs L permits

The B permit is the residence permit, usually issued for one year and renewable (five years for EU/EFTA nationals). The L permit is short-stay, up to one year and extendable to 24 months. Both depend on the employer's application and the quota. Cantonal fees run roughly CHF 50–150 plus SEM fees, and processing takes 2–6 months.

Who Switzerland actually accepts

The system favours senior researchers, elite tech talent, intra-company transfers and genuinely hard-to-find specialists. If you fit that profile, an employer who wants you will fight for a quota place. If you are mid-career, an EU/EFTA path (through a job in a neighbouring country or by studying first) is usually the stronger route, because a Swiss degree makes you a far more credible "specialist" for the quota and precedence tests.

The study route into Switzerland

Third-country students need a long-stay D visa with proof of funds of roughly CHF 21,000 per year, and may work up to 15 hours a week during term. After graduation you get up to six months to find a job; your employer then applies for a B permit under the quota. Study years do not count toward the 10-year C permit clock, so settlement still takes the full stretch of work years — but the degree is a real foot in the door. See our study in Switzerland guide for the university and cost details.

EU/EFTA and other routes

EU/EFTA nationals are covered by the 2002 free-movement agreement: no work permit and no quota, just registration with the commune, a 5-year B permit and a C permit after five years. Self-employed third-country nationals can apply for a discretionary permit under Article 19 FNIA by proving their activity serves Switzerland's economic interest (job creation, innovation, tax contribution), with incorporation requiring CHF 20,000 (GmbH) or CHF 100,000 (AG). Family reunification for B holders is possible after 12 months, with fees of roughly CHF 100–300 per family member.

How long until PR and citizenship?

Permanent residence (the C permit) comes after 10 years for most third-country nationals (5 for EU/EFTA nationals and some US/Canadian nationals under special treaties). Citizenship needs 10 years of continuous residence, a C permit, and integration including A2–B1 language skills, processed over 12–24 months across three levels of government. There is no retirement visa and no golden visa, so the honest paths are: exceptional employment, self-employment, study-then-work, EU/EFTA free movement, or family reunification. For the full detail on every permit, fee and the official sources, see our immigrate to Switzerland guide.

faq.q: Can I immigrate to Switzerland without a job offer?
faq.a: No for third-country nationals. An employer must apply for your permit through the canton, proving no Swiss or EU/EFTA candidate was available. There is no points-based independent route and no digital-nomad visa.

faq.q: Is there an EU Blue Card in Switzerland?
faq.a: No. Switzerland is not in the EU and has no EU Blue Card. Third-country admission runs through quotas (8,500 permits in 2026) and a case-by-case labour-market test, with no fixed salary threshold.

faq.q: How long does it take to get Swiss permanent residence?
faq.a: The C permit (permanent residence) comes after 10 years for most third-country nationals (5 for EU/EFTA nationals and some US/Canadian nationals). Citizenship needs 10 years of continuous residence plus integration including A2–B1 language.

faq.q: What are the Swiss work permit quotas for 2026?
faq.a: 8,500 permits for third-country nationals (4,500 B residence + 4,000 L short-stay), unchanged from 2025. Separate quotas cover EU/EFTA service providers (3,500) and UK nationals (3,500).

faq.q: Can I switch from a tourist visa to a work permit in Switzerland?
faq.a: No. The Schengen C visa is short-stay and cannot be converted into a work permit. A Swiss employer must apply for your B or L permit via the canton while you are outside the country.

posts.title: How to Immigrate to Italy (2026): EU Blue Card & Work Permits
posts.metaDescription: How to immigrate to Italy in 2026: the EU Blue Card (€35,500 salary), Decreto Flussi quotas, work visas and the 5-year path to PR.
posts.excerpt: The two real doors into Italy in 2026: the quota-free EU Blue Card for professionals and the Decreto Flussi lottery for other workers.
posts.bodyHtml:
Italy's immigration system has two very different doors. For qualified professionals, the EU Blue Card is fast, quota-free and available year-round, requiring a salary of around €35,500 and a valid job offer. For everyone else, the Decreto Flussi is an annual quota lottery that opens on a "click day" and typically fills within minutes. This guide explains both routes, plus the digital-nomad visa and the study-first path, so you know which door actually fits your profile before you start.

If you are a university-educated professional, or have five years of relevant experience, the Blue Card is almost always the smarter play than waiting for a quota window.

Key takeaways

  • The EU Blue Card is Italy's skilled route: quota-free, year-round, for a highly qualified job paying at least €35,000–35,500 gross a year (reduced to ~€28,200 in shortage sectors like ICT and healthcare).
  • The Decreto Flussi is the annual capped quota (around 150,000 slots in 2025) for seasonal, subordinate and trade work, applied for by employers on the click day.
  • Your employer secures a Nulla Osta (work authorisation) first; you then apply for a Type D work visa and convert it to a residence permit within eight working days of arrival.
  • The study-first route is often the most reliable: convert your student permit to a work permit any time, no quota window needed.
  • Permanent residence comes after 5 years of legal residence; citizenship after 10 (4 for EU citizens).

The EU Blue Card: Italy's skilled route

The Blue Card is for university-educated professionals or those with five years' professional experience equivalent to a higher-education qualification. You need a job offer for a highly qualified position with a contract of at least 12 months and a salary meeting the threshold: €35,000–35,500 gross per year (1.5x the national average), or around €28,200 in shortage sectors such as ICT and healthcare. The salary must be base salary, not bonuses, and must also meet the minimum set by the relevant collective agreement. Processing runs 60–120 days total (Nulla Osta 30–90 days), the permit lasts one to two years and renews up to four years and beyond, and spouses and children join with immediate work rights. After 18 months, Blue Card holders gain EU-wide mobility, and time on the card counts toward long-term residence.

The Decreto Flussi quota route

Each year a decree sets how many non-EU workers may enter Italy for employment, around 150,000 slots in 2025, split between seasonal, non-seasonal subordinate, self-employment and conversions. Employers submit on the "click day", first come, first served, and the window is often exhausted within minutes, which is why most successful applications are filed by an experienced Italian lawyer the moment it opens. Duration is usually two years for subordinate work, and it builds the residence history you need for PR after five years, though seasonal work does not lead to residence directly.

Digital nomad and other routes

The digital-nomad visa, introduced in 2024, suits highly skilled remote workers earning from abroad: roughly €28,000 a year in income, health insurance and accommodation proof, valid one year and renewable. The Italia Startup Visa is quota-free for founders of innovative startups, with a decision in about 90 days. Intra-company transfers and family reunification (spouses, minor children and dependent parents, with work rights) round out the picture. Retirees and people of independent means can use the elective residence visa, which requires passive income of roughly €31,000+ a year and allows no work.

The study-first route

International graduates of Italian universities can convert their student permit to a work permit at any time, with no Flussi window since the 2023 reform, and can take a 12-month job-search permit. Tuition at Italian public universities is low (often €1,000–3,000, and sometimes less), so studying first is both cheaper and strategically smarter than competing for quota places from abroad. See our study in Italy guide for the full picture.

Costs, PR and citizenship

Key 2026 fees: Type D work visa about €116, residence permit (permesso di soggiorno) around €70.50, and Schengen tourist visa €90. Permanent residence (Permesso di Soggiorno UE) comes after 5 years of continuous legal residence, and citizenship after 10 years (4 for EU citizens) with B1 Italian and a clean record. Italy permits dual nationality. For the complete breakdown of every route, fee and the official sources, see our immigrate to Italy guide.

faq.q: Can I get an Italian work visa without a degree?
faq.a: Yes. The EU Blue Card accepts five years of professional experience as equivalent to a higher-education qualification, especially for IT, engineering and senior management. The Decreto Flussi route also does not require a degree but is quota-capped.

faq.q: What is the difference between the EU Blue Card and Decreto Flussi?
faq.a: The Blue Card is quota-free, year-round and for qualified professionals above a salary threshold (about €35,500, or €28,200 in shortage sectors), with family work rights and faster processing. Decreto Flussi is the annual capped quota system for seasonal, trade and subordinate work.

faq.q: How long does the Italian Blue Card process take?
faq.a: About 2–4 months total: the Nulla Osta takes 30–90 days, then the Type D visa at the consulate, then conversion to the residence permit within 8 working days of arrival.

faq.q: Can my family live and work in Italy?
faq.a: Yes. EU Blue Card families get residence permits with immediate work rights, spouses can work without extra procedures, and children attend Italian public schools free. Family reunification also applies for spouses, minor children and dependent parents of residents.

faq.q: Can I switch from a tourist visa to a work visa in Italy?
faq.a: No. A Schengen C visa cannot be converted into a work or residence permit. You need a Nulla Osta obtained by your employer and a Type D work visa from an Italian consulate before you arrive. The main exception is converting a student permit to a work permit.

posts.title: New Zealand Student Visa 2026: Fees, Requirements & Costs
posts.metaDescription: The 2026 New Zealand student visa: NZ$850 fee, NZ$20,000 living-cost requirement, documents, work rights and application timeline.
posts.excerpt: Everything about the 2026 New Zealand student visa, including the NZ$850 fee, the NZ$20,000/year funds requirement and 25 hrs/week work rights.
posts.bodyHtml:
The New Zealand student visa is one of the most affordable and most strategically useful in the developed world. In 2026 the fee-paying student visa costs NZD $850, the living-cost proof is NZD $20,000 per year, and a Level 7+ New Zealand degree plugs directly into the Skilled Migrant and Green List residence systems. That combination of low entry cost and a clear path to residency makes New Zealand a standout choice for students who want to stay after they graduate. This guide covers the fee, the funds you must prove, the documents, the work rights and the timeline.

New Zealand is genuinely small: eight universities, around 5.2 million people, and a tight housing market in Auckland, but the system is engineered to fast-track skilled graduates toward residence.

Key takeaways

  • The fee-paying student visa costs NZD $850 (Pathway Student Visa NZD $750), non-refundable.
  • You must prove NZD $20,000 per year for living costs (about $1,667 a month for stays under a year) plus tuition, return travel and insurance, with funds ideally held for three-plus months.
  • You need an Offer of Place from an NZQA-registered (approved) education provider and mandatory medical and travel insurance.
  • Tertiary students can work 25 hours a week during term and full-time in scheduled holidays; master's-by-research and PhD students can work unlimited hours.
  • Processing takes about 8 weeks, so apply around four months before your course starts (main intakes: February and July).
  • An NZ bachelor's earns 5 of the 6 Skilled Migrant points needed; an NZ master's can earn 5–6 outright, making the degree a direct route toward residence.

Visa fee and costs for 2026

The fee-paying student visa is NZD $850, and the Pathway Student Visa (for study plans with an approved pathway provider) is NZD $750. On top of the visa you must show evidence of funds for: first-year tuition, living costs of NZD $20,000 per year, return travel and health insurance (around NZD $500–855 a year). University tuition for international undergraduates runs roughly NZD 26,000–47,000 a year, while polytechnics start around NZD 9,000, and international PhD students pay domestic-rate fees (about NZD 7,500–9,000).

Documents you need

Start with the Offer of Place from an NZQA-approved provider, since everything flows from it. Then prepare proof of funds with a clear, traceable history, valid passport, a genuine-intention statement (reason for study and return plans), an English test if required (IELTS 6.0–6.5 is the typical university bar; 5.5–6.0 for polytechnics), medical and travel insurance, and, where needed, an x-ray or medical certificate. Biometrics are part of the application for most nationalities.

Work rights while studying

Tertiary students on a student visa can work up to 25 hours a week during term and full-time during scheduled holidays. Students in master's-by-research and PhD programs can work unlimited hours, and secondary students in Years 12–13 can work up to 20 hours a week with permission. The New Zealand minimum wage sits around NZD $23.50–23.95 an hour, so part-time work makes a real dent in living costs.

After graduation: staying in New Zealand

After study you can apply for the Post Study Work Visa (NZD $1,670): Level 7 degrees of 30+ weeks earn 1–3 years, and master's and PhD graduates get three years. A new 6-month Short-term Graduate Work Visa also launches on 16 November 2026. The migration payoff is the real story: an NZ bachelor's earns 5 of the 6 points in the Skilled Migrant system, an NZ master's can earn 5–6 outright, and NZ qualifications get a +1 point bonus over overseas ones from August 2026. Green List occupations (IT, engineering, health, construction) can go straight to residence. See our immigrate to New Zealand guide for the full points breakdown.

Timeline and tips

Allow about 8 weeks for processing and apply around four months before your course starts, targeting the February or July intakes. Apply to an NZQA-approved provider early, because the Offer of Place gates everything else. For a fuller comparison of costs, universities and cities, see our study in New Zealand guide, and for country-by-country visa requirements, the visa guidance page.

faq.q: How much money do I need for a New Zealand student visa?
faq.a: NZD $20,000 per year of living costs (about $1,667 a month for stays under a year) plus first-year tuition, return travel and insurance. Funds should be genuinely yours with a traceable history, ideally three-plus months in the bank.

faq.q: How much does the New Zealand student visa cost in 2026?
faq.a: NZD $850 for the fee-paying student visa, or NZD $750 for the Pathway Student Visa. This is well below Australia's AUD $2,500 student visa fee.

faq.q: Can I work while studying in New Zealand?
faq.a: Yes. Tertiary students can work up to 25 hours a week during term and full-time in scheduled holidays. Master's-by-research and PhD students can work unlimited hours, and secondary students in Years 12–13 can work up to 20 hours a week with permission.

faq.q: Is a New Zealand degree good for permanent residence?
faq.a: Very. An NZ bachelor's earns 5 of the 6 Skilled Migrant points needed, an NZ master's can earn 5–6 outright, NZ qualifications get a +1 point bonus from August 2026, and a Level 7+ qualification in a Green List occupation is one of the fastest residence paths in the developed world.

faq.q: When should I apply for a New Zealand student visa?
faq.a: Allow about 8 weeks for processing, so apply around four months before your course starts (main intakes in February and July). Get your Offer of Place from an NZQA-approved provider first, since everything flows from that.
